문제.nuance: 문제(問題, 'ask + topic') has two everyday senses English keeps apart: a trouble or difficulty ('we have a problem') AND a question on a test or exercise ('problem 3'). Crucially, both are solved with the same verb 풀다 (literally 'to untie/loosen') — 문제를 풀다 works for a math item and for a real-life difficulty alike, where English would switch to 'answer' vs 'solve.' Other key partners: 문제가 생기다 (a problem arises), 문제가 되다 (to become an issue), and the handy one-word 문제없어요 ('no problem'). Contrast 문제 with 질문 (a question you ASK someone to get information) — a test 문제 is a problem to solve, but raising your hand to ask is 질문하다, not 문제하다. The English-speaker pitfall is the subject/object split: existence and arising take 이 (문제가 있다/생기다), but solving takes 를 (문제를 풀다) — learners often say 문제가 풀어요.

걷다.nuance: 걷다 means to walk on foot and is a ㄷ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ softens to ㄹ, so the 요-form is 걸어요 (not 걷어요) and the past is 걸었어요. Before a consonant ending the ㄷ stays put, so the formal form remains 걷습니다 and you say 걷지 마세요, 걷고 싶어요. The nearest relative is 산책하다 ('take a stroll'): 걷다 is the raw act of walking anywhere, while 산책하다 implies a leisurely walk for pleasure, so 'I walk to work' is 걸어서 출근해요, never 산책해서 출근해요. The trap for English speakers is that 걷다 doesn't take an object the way 'walk the dog' does — Korean uses 산책시키다 for that, and the path you walk takes 을/를 (공원을 걸어요), so don't reach for 에. Also remember 걸어서 ('on foot') is one fixed chunk for describing how you travel.

도착하다.nuance: 도착하다 is Sino-Korean 到着(도착: 到 reach + 着 attach/touch down) plus 하다 — the moment of REACHING and touching a destination. Its mirror is 출발하다(depart), and the key is the particle: you arrive AT a place with 에 (호텔에 도착해요), whereas 출발하다 leaves FROM a place with 에서. Don't confuse it with 들어가다/들어오다(enter): 도착하다 is reaching the destination's threshold, not stepping inside a building. As a 하다 verb, 하 + 아 fuses to 해 (도착해요) and the short negative and inability split the noun off: 도착 안 해요, 도착 못 해요. The classic English-speaker error is copying 'arrive at' as 에서 — 'at' here is the static endpoint 에, so 공항에 도착해요, and 공항에서 도착해요 is wrong.
도착하다.explanation: 도착하다 (dochakada) = "to arrive". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 도착해요 plus one useful sentence like 공항에 도착해요 ("I arrive at the airport."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 도착하고 싶어요 for what you want, 도착할 수 있어요 for what you can, 도착 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help.

포기하다.nuance: 포기하다 = to give up, abandon, or relinquish a goal, plan, claim, or even a person. The hanja 抛棄 is vivid: 抛 'to throw/hurl away' + 棄 'to discard, abandon', so the image is hurling something aside and walking off — a decisive letting-go, not a gentle fade. Contrast 포기하다 (stop pursuing a goal entirely) with 그만두다 (stop/quit an ongoing activity — a job, a habit) and with 단념하다 (a more bookish 'resign oneself to abandoning hope'); in speech 포기하다 is the everyday choice. Grammar: it pairs with 을/를 (목표를 포기하다) or with 는 거 / 는 걸 (사는 걸 포기하다 = 'give up on buying'). Culturally the word is loaded: N포세대, the 'give-up generation', names young Koreans said to have surrendered dating, marriage, and kids to economic pressure. English-speaker pitfall: the negative is 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), NOT 안 포기해.

운동.nuance: 운동 is Sino-Korean, 運動 ('move-motion'), and is the umbrella word for physical exercise; it normally appears as 운동하다 (운동을 해요). Crucially it is NOT counted or pluralized like English 'a workout' — you don't say 운동들 for several sessions; you say 운동을 자주 해요. The nearest relative is 스포츠 (a borrowed word for organized sports as a category, e.g. watching 스포츠 on TV), whereas 운동 is the act of exercising your own body, so '운동선수' = athlete but '스포츠 경기' = a sports match. The very same 運動 also means a social 'movement/campaign' (민주화 운동 the democracy movement), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') by analogy with 'make exercise' — Korean uses the light verb 하다; and remember the desire ending goes on the verb (운동하고 싶어요), never on the bare noun.
운동.explanation: 운동 (undong) means "exercise". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 운동을 해요 ("I exercise"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 운동 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
운동.shortExplanation: 운동 means "exercise" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 운동을 만들어요 by translating 'do/make exercise' literally — 만들다 means physically craft something; the correct light verb is 하다, so 운동을 해요.
Attaching the want-ending to the noun as 운동 싶어요 — -고 싶다 only fastens to a verb stem, so it must be 운동하고 싶어요 / 운동을 하고 싶어요.
Using 운동들 to mean several workouts — 운동 is non-count here; say 운동을 여러 번 해요 or 자주 운동해요 instead.

cluster.rule: They mean the same thing and are almost always swappable; 같이 is what people actually say out loud every day, while 함께 sounds a bit warmer and more polished, so it turns up in writing, invitations and slogans.

쉽다.nuance: 쉽다 is ㅂ irregular: 쉬워요, 쉬운. It helps learners talk about difficulty level, but the opposite 어렵다 is often needed in the same lesson.
쉽다.explanation: 쉽다 (swipda) = "to be easy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쉬워요 ("It is easy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쉽다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
쉽다.shortExplanation: 쉽다 means "to be easy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

쉽다 becomes 쉬워요, not 쉽어요.

conjugationTips.title: Describing a noun: ㄴ/은 vs ㄹ/을
conjugationTips.body: To put 쉽다 in front of a noun, use the ㄴ/은 form for how something is right now: 쉬운 것 ("a easy thing"). The ㄹ/을 form points to something that will or might become that way later. So 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot now, but 뜨거울 물 is water that will be hot — same adjective, different time feeling. For everyday description, reach for the ㄴ/은 form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㅂ → 우
conjugationTips.body: 쉽다 is a ㅂ-irregular word. Before a vowel ending the final ㅂ turns into 우, so the polite form is 쉬워요 — not a literal ㅂ + 어요. The same change gives the noun-describing form (맵다 → 매운, 쉽다 → 쉬운). Anchor on 쉬워요 and build the rest from it.

ex.en: I think this method might be possible.

가능하다.nuance: 가능하다 (可能, 可 'can/permissible' + 能 'ability') means 'possible / doable / available', and it is wonderfully practical for daily service questions — 예약 가능해요? ('Is a reservation possible?'), 카드 가능해요? ('Can I pay by card?'). In these, a noun sits directly before it and it neatly replaces a longer '-ㄹ 수 있다' clause, sounding crisp and businesslike. The softener 가능하면 ('if possible') makes requests polite, and the fixed frame 가능한 한 + adjective/adverb means 'as ~ as possible' (가능한 한 빨리 'as soon as possible') — note this is different from 가능한 N ('a possible N'). Its antonym is 불가능하다. One pitfall: while 가능하다 and '-ㄹ 수 있다' both render English 'can', '-ㄹ 수 있다' attaches to a verb stem describing an action you're able to do (갈 수 있어요 'I can go'), whereas 가능하다 attaches to a noun or stands alone judging feasibility — don't merge them into 갈 가능해요.
가능하다.explanation: 가능하다 (ganeunghada) = "to be possible". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: N 가능하다 ("N is possible / available") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가능하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
가능하다.shortExplanation: 가능하다 means "to be possible" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 가능하다 (possible) with its 불- prefixed antonym 불가능하다 (impossible).
Mixing 가능한 N ('a possible N') with the 'as ~ as possible' meaning — for the latter the set form is 가능한 한 + adjective/adverb (가능한 한 천천히 'as slowly as possible').
Gluing 가능하다 onto a verb like '갈 가능해요' — to express ability with a verb use '-ㄹ 수 있다' (갈 수 있어요); 가능하다 follows a noun or stands alone.

usagePhrases.note: drops 이/가 in shop talk, e.g. 예약 가능해요?

회의.nuance: 회의 (漢字 會議, 會 'gather' + 議 'discuss') is a formal, work-style meeting where people gather to discuss and decide something — a board meeting, a team sync, a planning session. The near-synonym learners reach for is 모임, but 모임 is a social get-together (a dinner, a club, friends meeting up) with no agenda, so calling drinks with friends a 회의 sounds robotic; conversely calling a budget review a 모임 sounds too loose. It pairs naturally with 회의를 하다 (hold), 회의에 들어가다 (go into), 회의가 길어지다 (run long). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you are *in* a meeting as a location, so the action takes 회의에서, but you *enter* a meeting with 회의에 들어가다 — and never confuse 회의 with the look-alike 회사 (company) or 회비 (membership fee).
회의.explanation: 회의 (hoeui) means "meeting". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회의가 있어요. ("There is a meeting."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 회의 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
회의.shortExplanation: 회의 means "meeting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 친구하고 회의했어요 for hanging out with friends — 회의 implies a formal agenda; for a casual gathering say 친구하고 모였어요 or use 모임.
Using 회의에 for where talking happens, as in 회의에 이야기했어요 — the location of an action needs 에서: 회의에서 이야기했어요. Reserve 회의에 for 들어가다/참석하다.
Mixing up 회의 with 회사; 회사에 가요 means go to the company/office, while 회의에 가요 means go to the meeting.

usagePhrases.note: Existence with 있다 plus subject 이/가 — the default way to announce a meeting on the calendar.
회의에 들어가다 'enter a meeting' is the set phrase; use 에 here, not 에서, because you are moving in.
회의 takes 하다 to become a verb; 회의하다 = the act of meeting, distinct from the event noun.
Bare noun + 시간 forms a time phrase; no particle between 회의 and 시간.

examples.en: I have two meetings today.
examples.note: Counts meetings with 개; 회의가 (subject) is what 있다 describes.

examples.en: We decided a new plan in the meeting.

ex.ko: 메시지는 자주 보내지만 전화는 잘 안 해요.
ex.en: I send messages often, but I do not call much.
ex.note: 은/는 makes the contrast visible.

메시지.nuance: 메시지 is the loanword from English 'message' and covers chat/app messages broadly (a KakaoTalk message, a DM); the everyday near-synonym 문자 (literally 文字 'letters/characters') specifically means an SMS text, so '문자 보내' = 'text me' while '메시지' is the wider term. There's also 카톡, the verb-able brand shorthand for a KakaoTalk message, used constantly in real life (카톡 보낼게 'I'll Kakao you'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, the recipient is marked with 한테/에게 ('to a person'), not the English bare object — 친구한테 메시지를 보내다, where 친구한테 = 'to my friend' and 메시지를 is the thing sent; second, the message arriving uses intransitive 오다 with 이/가 (메시지가 오다), but you sending it uses 보내다 with 을/를 (메시지를 보내다). Don't carry the English 'send him a message' double-object pattern straight over.
메시지.explanation: "message" is 메시지 (mesiji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 메시지를 보내요 ("I send a message"). Watch the particle attached to 메시지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
메시지.shortExplanation: 메시지 means "message" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 메시지가 보내요 for 'I send a message'. 보내다 is transitive: 메시지를 보내요.
Marking the recipient with the object marker, e.g. 친구를 메시지를 보내요. The person who receives it takes 한테/에게: 친구한테 메시지를 보내요.
Treating 메시지 and 문자 as identical. 문자 specifically means an SMS text; for that, '문자 보낼게' is the natural phrase, while 메시지 is the broader word for any app message.

examples.en: Please send me a message.
examples.note: -아/어 주세요 = polite request

ex.en: Oh, they have already arrived.
ex.note: 벌써 pairs well with surprise or realization.

벌써.nuance: 벌써 means 'already', but its core flavor is SURPRISE that something happened sooner than you expected — 'wow, already?'. Compare its near-twin 이미: 이미 is the neutral 'already / by now' that simply reports a completed fact (이미 끝났어요 'it's already finished', stating it), whereas 벌써 adds the emotional jolt (벌써 끝났어요? 'it's done already?!'). So a flat report prefers 이미; an astonished reaction prefers 벌써. It naturally rides with past tense and with 다('all'), and often co-occurs with the exclamatory endings -네요/-군요. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't pair 벌써 with the future — English 'already' can sit oddly with plans, but 벌써 is about something that has ALREADY occurred, so it takes past/completed verbs (벌써 갔어요), not 벌써 갈 거예요. Use 곧/이미 곧 logic for 'soon' instead.
벌써.explanation: "already" is 벌써 (beolsseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벌써 왔어요 ("you're here already?!"). Watch the particle attached to 벌써 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
벌써.shortExplanation: 벌써 means "already" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Attaching 벌써 to future actions: 벌써 갈 거예요 is wrong. 벌써 needs a completed event — 벌써 갔어요 ('already left').
Swapping in 벌써 where you only want a neutral report. To plainly state a fact, 이미 is better; 벌써 injects surprise you may not intend.
Word order: 끝났어요 벌써 follows English; Korean puts it first — 벌써 끝났어요.

examples.en: Is it lunchtime already?
examples.note: Simple: 벌써 voices surprise that time passed fast.

examples.en: I've already finished that book.
examples.note: Everyday: with past tense + 다, 벌써 stresses 'done sooner than expected'.

examples.en: The snow has already melted. It must be spring.
examples.note: Real situation: 벌써 + the surprise-marker -네요 conveys mild astonishment.

cluster.title: 벌써 vs 이미 vs 아직
cluster.rule: 벌써 and 이미 differ in tone, not timing: 벌써 reacts with surprise ("already?!"), while 이미 just reports a settled fact. 아직 is the opposite pole — "not yet" with a negative verb, "still" with a positive one.

members.hint: "already?!" with the surprise built in

"not yet" with 안, "still" without

ex.ko: 서류를 미리 준비했더라면 접수를 놓치지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had prepared the documents in advance, I would not have missed the application.
ex.note: 준비했더라면 turns a practical mistake into a counterfactual condition.

준비하다.nuance: 준비하다 comes from 한자 準備 (準 'standard, level' + 備 'provide, equip'), literally 'get equipped to standard' — to ready things or yourself beforehand. It naturally collocates with events and outcomes: 시험을 준비하다, 여행을 준비하다, 저녁을 준비하다, 마음의 준비. Compare 마련하다 ('arrange/procure' funds or a place — 집을 마련하다) and 챙기다 ('gather up, pack' your own belongings — 여권 챙겼어? = did you grab your passport?); 준비하다 is the broad 'prepare,' while 챙기다 zooms in on not forgetting items. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'prepare FOR the exam' tempts 시험에 준비하다, but Korean treats the exam as a direct object — 시험을 준비하다. Also don't reach for 만들다 'make' when you only mean getting ready. As a 하다 verb, negate inside (준비 안 해요), and its passive 준비되다 ('be ready') is everywhere: 준비됐어요.
준비하다.explanation: 준비하다 (junbihada) = "to prepare". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 준비해요 plus one useful sentence like 저녁을 준비해요. ("I prepare dinner."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 준비하고 싶어요 for what you want, 준비할 수 있어요 for what you can, 준비 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
준비하다.shortExplanation: 준비하다 means "to prepare" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 준비하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 준비해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Wrong particle: '시험에 준비해요' for 'prepare for the exam.' Korean uses the object marker: 시험을 준비해요.
Using 만들다 (make) for getting ready: 'dinner is being prepared' is 저녁을 준비해요, not 저녁을 만들어요 unless you stress the cooking itself.
Saying '준비해요' to answer 'Are you ready?' The state 'I'm ready' is the passive 준비됐어요 / 준비됐어; 준비해요 means the act of preparing.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 준비하다 becomes 준비할 수 있어요 ("can") and 준비할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Meal + 을/를 + 준비하다; getting food ready.

examples.en: Did you get the food ready?
examples.note: Casual; 밥 stands in for 'a meal' generally.

examples.en: I have to prepare for tomorrow's presentation.
examples.note: 준비해야 하다 expresses the obligation to get ready.

examples.en: Prepare the gift in advance (and keep it ready).
examples.note: 준비해 두다 = prepare and leave set; 미리 reinforces 'ahead of time.'

ex.en: I will check the order right away.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-verb-482.

확인하다.nuance: 확인하다 (確認하다, 確 'certain/firm' + 認 'recognize') means to check, verify, or confirm that something is correct or true — facts, times, reservations, messages — making sure reality matches what you expect. The crucial contrast is with 찾다, which English 'check' can blur: 찾다 is 'to look FOR / search' something not yet located (열쇠를 찾다, 'look for the keys'), whereas 확인하다 is 'to verify' something you can already see (열쇠가 있는지 확인하다, 'check whether the keys are there'). It also differs from 알아보다 ('look into/inquire to find out', 가격을 알아보다). It's a regular noun+하다 verb: 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요, past 확인했어요, with 안/못 splitting before 하다 (확인 안 해요, 확인 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'check the box' or 'check off' is NOT 확인하다 — ticking a box is 체크하다/표시하다; and 'check out a book/check out (a hotel)' uses 빌리다 or 체크아웃하다, not 확인하다, which strictly means 'verify/confirm'.
확인하다.explanation: "to check" in Korean is 확인하다 (hwaginhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 확인해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 확인하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이메일을 확인하다 ("to check email") — then reshape the same stem into 확인하고 싶어요 (desire), 확인할 수 있어요 (ability), and 확인 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
확인하다.shortExplanation: 확인하다 means "to check" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 확인하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 확인해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 확인하다 for 'look for/search' — finding something lost is 찾다 (지갑을 찾다); 확인하다 verifies something you can already check.
Saying 확인하다 for 'check (tick) a box' — that's 체크하다/표시하다; 확인하다 means confirm/verify, not mark.
Splitting as 못 확인해요 — the standard negative for a noun+하다 verb is 확인 못 해요 / 확인 안 해요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 확인하다 becomes 확인할 수 있어요 ("can") and 확인할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 확인하다 = verify/confirm the content; 이메일을 확인해요

examples.en: I check my email.
examples.note: Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요

examples.en: I have to check the time before leaving.
examples.note: -기 전에 ('before doing'); 확인해야 해요 expresses obligation

examples.en: Please check whether this address is correct.
examples.note: -는지 embeds the yes/no question; 확인해 주세요 requests the favor

ex.ko: 버스를 놓치지 않았더라면 늦지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had not missed the bus, I would not have been late.
ex.note: Use 놓치다 for transport, chances, deadlines, and timing.

놓치다.nuance: 놓치다 is for missing something you were actively trying to catch or hold — a bus, a train, a flight, a chance, or even the thread of a conversation (요점을 놓치다 = 'miss the point') — and it always takes a 을/를 object. Its make-up shows the meaning: 놓다 ('to let go/release') + 치다, so it literally pictures something slipping out of your grasp. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is using it for missing a *person*: English 'I miss you' is NOT 놓치다 — that is 보고 싶다 ('want to see'), so 엄마가 보고 싶어요, never 엄마를 놓쳐요. Contrast 놓치다 ('fail to catch what was within reach') with 지나가다/지나치다 ('let pass / pass by'): you 놓치다 a bus you ran for, but a chance that quietly 지나가다 simply went by. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 놓치 + 어 → 놓쳐요, and it frequently appears alongside 늦다 ('be late').
놓치다.explanation: 놓치다 (nochida) = "to miss". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 놓쳐요 plus one useful sentence like 버스를 놓쳤어요 ("I missed the bus"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 놓치고 싶어요 for what you want, 놓칠 수 있어요 for what you can, 놓칠 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
놓치다.shortExplanation: 놓치다 means "to miss" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놓치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놓쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
To say you miss a PERSON, use 보고 싶다, not 놓치다 — 놓치다 is only for missing a bus, train, chance, etc.
Don't drop the object marker: it's 버스를 놓쳤어요, since 놓치다 is transitive and needs a 을/를 object.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 놓치다 becomes 놓칠 수 있어요 ("can") and 놓칠 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = fail to catch a bus/train/flight; the thing missed takes 을/를.

examples.en: I just missed the bus
examples.note: The most typical use, for transport you failed to catch.

examples.en: I was late because I missed the subway
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 늦다 in everyday excuses (-아서 gives the reason).

examples.ko: 이런 좋은 기회를 놓치면 안 돼요
examples.romanization: ireon joeun gihoereul notchimyeon an dwaeyo
examples.en: You shouldn't miss a good chance like this
examples.note: Opportunities use 놓치다 too; -면 안 되다 gives the 'mustn't' warning.

ex.en: It has been six months since I started learning Korean.
ex.note: 배우기 시작하다 marks the beginning of the learning action.

배우다.nuance: 배우다 means 'to learn / acquire a skill or subject' and takes the object marker 을/를: 한국어를 배워요. It is a regular verb, but the stem ends in the vowel 우, so when 어요 attaches the two vowels contract into 워 — 배우 + 어요 → 배워요 (not 배우어요), past 배웠어요. The natural partner verb is 가르치다 ('to teach'), the giving side of the same act; and the person you learn from takes 한테/에게서 (사람) — 선생님한테 배워요 — never the place particle 에서 for the source. Contrast 배우다 with 공부하다 (工夫하다, 'to study'): 공부하다 is the effort of studying (sitting down, reviewing, hitting the books), while 배우다 is the result of acquiring a skill or being taught it, often from someone. So you 공부하다 for an exam at your desk but 배우다 the piano from a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is writing the uncontracted 배우어요, and saying 학원에서 배우다 to mean 'learn from the academy' — 에서 marks where, while the human source must take 한테/에게서.
배우다.explanation: 배우다 (baeuda) = "to learn". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 배워요 plus one useful sentence like 한국어를 배워요 ("I learn Korean"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 배우고 싶어요 for what you want, 배울 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 배워요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help.
배우다.shortExplanation: 배우다 means "to learn" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 배우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 배워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the uncontracted 배우어요 — the 우 + 어요 contracts, so the polite present is 배워요 (past 배웠어요).
Confusing 배우다 with 공부하다 — 공부하다 is the act of studying/reviewing; 배우다 is acquiring or being taught a skill. Use 시험공부를 해요 for exam prep, 피아노를 배워요 for taking lessons.
Marking the person you learn from with 에서 — a human source takes 한테/에게서: 선생님한테 배워요, not 선생님에서.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 배우다 becomes 배울 수 있어요 ("can") and 배울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the subject/skill learned takes the object marker 을/를

examples.en: I learn Korean.
examples.note: two vowels contract: 배우 + 어요 → 배워요

examples.en: These days I'm learning guitar from a friend.
examples.note: source person takes 한테; 고 있다 = ongoing

examples.ko: 저는 운전을 배워서 회사에 차로 가고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun unjeoneul baewoseo hoesae charo gago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to learn to drive and go to work by car.
examples.note: real goal-linked sentence; 배워서 connects reason to plan

ex.en: If I had solved the last question, I would have passed.
ex.note: 합격하다 belongs naturally in exam-regret counterfactuals.

합격하다.nuance: 합격하다 is Sino-Korean 合格 — 合 'meet/match' + 格 'standard' — literally 'meet the standard', i.e. clear a cut-off and pass a test, interview, or admissions screen. Its opposite is 불합격하다 (不合格) or, much more colloquially, 떨어지다 'to fall/drop' (시험에 떨어졌어요 = I failed/flunked). Don't confuse 합격하다 with 통과하다 'to pass through': 통과하다 is moving past a checkpoint or a bill passing, while 합격하다 specifically means meeting a qualifying standard. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'pass THE exam' (object) makes learners write 시험을 합격하다, but Korean uses 에 — 시험에 합격하다 — because you're 'matching up TO the standard'. Note also 합격하다 (verb) vs 합격 (the noun, 'a pass/acceptance'): the noun is what you put on banners — 합격 축하해! As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (합격해요, 합격했어요, formal 합격합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (합격 안 해요, 합격 못 해요).
합격하다.explanation: "to pass an exam" in Korean is 합격하다 (hapgyeokada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 합격해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 합격하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 시험에 합격하다 ("to pass the exam / make the cut") — then reshape the same stem into 합격하고 싶어요 (desire), 합격할 수 있어요 (ability), and 합격 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
합격하다.shortExplanation: 합격하다 means "to pass an exam" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 합격하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 합격해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 시험을 합격했어요 because English treats the exam as a direct object — Korean marks it with 에: 시험에 합격했어요.
Using 합격하다 to mean a course or class 'passed' in the sense of finishing it — for clearing a checkpoint generally use 통과하다; 합격하다 = meeting a qualifying standard.
Forming 'I failed' as 합격 안 했어요, which sounds oddly neutral ('didn't pass') — the natural opposite Koreans say is 떨어졌어요 (시험에 떨어졌어요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 합격하다 becomes 합격할 수 있어요 ("can") and 합격할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not pass an exam.
I want to pass an exam.
I have to pass an exam.
to pass the exam / make the cut
usagePhrases.note: what you pass takes 에: 시험에 합격해요 (NOT 시험을)

examples.en: I passed the exam!
examples.note: Use 에 for the thing passed; the past 합격했어요 reports the result

examples.en: This time I really want to pass.
examples.note: 꼭 = for sure/without fail; 이번에는 = this time around

examples.ko: 공부를 안 하면 합격 못 해요.
examples.romanization: gongbureul an hamyeon hapgyeong mo taeyo.
examples.en: If you don't study, you can't pass.
examples.note: ~면 = if; impossible form splits: 합격 못 해요

ex.ko: 조금만 일찍 도착했더라면 시험을 볼 수 있었을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had arrived just a little earlier, I could have taken the exam.
ex.note: 시험을 보다 is the fixed phrase for taking an exam.

시험.nuance: 시험 is Sino-Korean 試驗 — 試 'try/test' + 驗 'examine', literally 'a trial examination'. The collocation English speakers must memorize is 시험을 보다 — Koreans 'see' an exam, they do not 'do' it, so 시험을 하다 is wrong. Passing and failing are vivid metaphors with the particle 에: 시험에 붙다 (literally 'stick to the exam') = pass, 시험에 떨어지다 ('fall off the exam') = fail — note these take 에, not 을. Contrast 시험 with 퀴즈(quiz, a small in-class test) and with 검사(檢査, an inspection/medical test like 건강 검사): a graded school test is always 시험, never 퀴즈 unless it is a tiny informal one. The classic 직역 trap is 'take an exam' → 시험을 가지다/취하다 ✗ (English 'take' never transfers); and learners often write 시험을 통과하다, which is understandable but bookish — the everyday word is 붙다.
시험.explanation: 시험 (siheom) = "exam". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험을 보다 ("take an exam") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시험, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
시험.shortExplanation: 시험 means "exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시험을 하다 instead of 시험을 보다. Koreans 'see/look at' an exam (보다); 하다 does not collocate with 시험.
Using 를 for pass/fail: 시험을 붙다 ✗. The verbs 붙다/떨어지다 take 에 — 시험에 붙다/떨어지다.
Translating 'take the exam' as 시험을 가지다 ('have/hold'). English 'take' is not literal here; the only natural verb is 보다.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed verb is 보다 (literally 'see'), never 하다
Existence/scheduling; the exam is the subject, so 이
붙다 'stick' = pass, 떨어지다 'fall' = fail; both take 에
기말(期末) = end of term; cf. 중간 시험 = midterm

examples.en: Is there an exam tomorrow?
examples.note: Casual; 있어요 used for a scheduled event existing

examples.en: I took the Korean exam yesterday.
examples.note: 봤어요 = past of 보다; the set phrase 시험을 보다

examples.en: I studied hard so I passed the exam.
examples.note: Pass = 시험에 붙다; note the particle is 에, not 를

ex.en: For my health, I decided to walk every day.
ex.note: Noun + 을 위해 is the noun version of V-기 위해.

건강.nuance: 건강 is Sino-Korean 健康, where 健 means 'sturdy/robust' and 康 means 'peaceful/well,' together the sound, robust state of body and mind. It splits into a noun and an adjective: the noun 건강 ('health') pairs with 좋다/나쁘다 (good/bad) — never 높다/낮다 (high/low), which is the typical English-influenced slip from 'high level of health' — and you actively mind it with 챙기다 (건강을 챙기다, 'look after your health'); the adjective 건강하다 means 'to be healthy' (저는 건강해요 = 'I'm healthy'). Its honorific imperative 건강하세요 is a beloved set phrase, a warm farewell/blessing meaning 'stay healthy,' especially said to elders and at New Year. A near-synonym is 컨디션 (a loanword from 'condition') — but 컨디션 is your day-to-day fitness/energy level (오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아 = 'I'm not feeling great today'), whereas 건강 is your overall, long-term state of wellness; don't swap them.
건강.explanation: 건강 (geongang) = "health". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 건강이 좋아요 ("my health is good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 건강, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
건강.shortExplanation: 건강 means "health" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 건강이 높아요 for good health: health is 좋다/나쁘다, so it must be 건강이 좋아요.
Confusing 건강 with 컨디션: long-term wellness is 건강; today's energy/feeling is 컨디션.
Saying 건강이세요 instead of 건강하세요: the blessing comes from the adjective 건강하다, giving 건강하세요.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다, not 높다, describes good health
챙기다 = take care of, mind one's health

examples.en: Health is the most important thing.
examples.note: Simple: 건강이 + adjective, the core 'health is X' frame.

examples.ko: 요즘 운동을 시작해서 건강이 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum undongeul sijakaeseo geongangi mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I started exercising lately, so my health has improved a lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 운동을 시작하다 + 건강이 좋아지다 (improve).

examples.en: Grandma, please always stay healthy and live a long, long life.
examples.note: Real-situation: honorific 건강하시다 + 사세요 as a warm blessing.

ex.en: I am building a habit of listening every day.
ex.note: -는 습관 naturally describes repeated behavior.

습관.nuance: 습관 (習慣, 習 'to practice/learn' + 慣 'to grow accustomed') frames a habit as something drilled in until it feels natural, and it leans slightly formal and neutral. The key contrast is 습관 vs 버릇: 습관 is a broad, often deliberate routine (early rising, daily exercise, good study habits), while 버릇 is colloquial and usually a quirky or annoying unconscious tic — nail-biting, leg-shaking, a child's bad manners. Crucially, scolding a child you say 버릇없다 ('has no manners / is rude'), never 습관없다. Both pair with 고치다 ('fix') for breaking them and 들이다/생기다 for forming them (습관을 들이다 = cultivate a habit; 습관이 생기다 = a habit forms). To say you have one, use 습관이 있다. Pitfall: English 'I have a habit of doing X' must use the verb's -는 present-modifier form before 습관: 일찍 자는 습관 (the habit of sleeping early), not 일찍 자기 습관. Also do not use 가지다 here — habits 있다/되다/생기다, they are not 'had' with 가지다.
습관.explanation: 습관 (seupgwan) means "habit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이것은 좋은 습관이에요. ("This is a good habit."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 습관 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
습관.shortExplanation: 습관 means "habit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forming 'have a habit of ~ing' wrongly: 운동하기 습관 is broken. Use the -는 modifier: 운동하는 습관이 있어요.
Using 습관 for a child's rudeness. 'That kid is rude/ill-mannered' is 그 아이는 버릇이 없어요, not 습관이 없어요.
Saying 습관을 가지고 있어요 by translating 'have a habit'. The idiomatic verb is 있다 or 되다: 습관이 있어요 / 습관이 됐어요.

usagePhrases.note: 좋은/나쁜 + 습관 describes the quality of a habit

usagePhrases.en: I want to fix a bad habit.
usagePhrases.note: 습관을 고치다 = 'correct/break a habit'; 고치다 = repair
습관이 되다 = 'turn into a habit', now automatic

usagePhrases.en: I have a habit of going to bed early.
usagePhrases.note: verb + -는 + 습관이 있다 = 'have the habit of ~ing'

examples.en: I have a habit of exercising every morning.
examples.note: -는 습관이 있다 is the frame for stating any routine

examples.en: I changed my coffee-drinking habit.
examples.note: 습관을 바꾸다 = 'change a habit' (swap it), milder than 고치다

examples.en: I can't break my nail-biting habit.
examples.note: Here a small bad tic is a 버릇, not 습관 — note the register difference

ex.ko: 그때 선택을 바꿨더라면 지금 상황이 달라졌을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had changed my choice then, the situation would be different now.
ex.note: 달라졌을 거예요 is a natural result clause for counterfactuals.

달라지다.nuance: 달라지다 spotlights the before-and-after gap: something is now clearly unlike how it used to be, which makes it the everyday verb for noticing change in a person's looks, mood, or a situation. It's the inchoative of the adjective 다르다 (to be different) — 다르 + -아지다 'become' — and that origin is the #1 pitfall: 다르다 states a static difference between two things (A는 B와 달라요 = A is different from B), while 달라지다 is the dynamic act of becoming different over time (분위기가 달라졌어요 = the mood changed). It overlaps with 변하다 and 바뀌다, but the dividing line is focus: 달라지다 = 'the result looks different now,' 변하다 = 'the inner nature transformed,' 바뀌다 = 'one thing got swapped for another.' Both 달라지다 and the thing changing take 이/가; the form 달라져요 comes from -지다 verbs taking 어 in the 요-form (지+어 → 져).
달라지다.explanation: 달라지다 (dallajida) = "to become different, to change". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 달라져요 plus one useful sentence like 분위기가 완전히 달라졌어요. ("The atmosphere became completely different."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 달라지고 싶어요 for what you want, 달라질 수 있어요 for what you can, 달라질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
달라지다.shortExplanation: 달라지다 means "to become different, to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 달라지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 달라져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 다르다 — 다르다 is an adjective for a static difference (저는 형과 성격이 달라요), while 달라지다 is a verb for becoming different (성격이 달라졌어요).
It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요. To deliberately change something, use 바꾸다.
Don't say the present as 달라요 when you mean 'is changing'; 달라요 = 'is different (now)', 달라지고 있어요 = 'is becoming different'.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 달라지다 becomes 달라질 수 있어요 ("can") and 달라질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not become different, to change.
I want to become different, to change.
I can become different, to change.
I have to become different, to change.

usagePhrases.note: 달라지다 = end up noticeably different from before. Built from 다르다 (be different) + -아지다.

examples.en: Did you cut your hair? You look different.
examples.note: Great compliment-ish line — 느낌이 달라지다 = the vibe/impression changed.

examples.en: Now that I've lived here, my thinking has changed a lot.
examples.note: Use for gradual inner change — 생각이/가치관이 달라지다.

examples.en: The rules will be different starting next year.
examples.note: Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.

ex.ko: 조금만 일찍 나왔으면 버스를 놓치지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had left just a little earlier, I would not have missed the bus.
ex.note: 조금만 일찍 is a very natural regret chunk.

일찍.nuance: 일찍 means 'early' in the sense of an EARLY POINT IN TIME — early hour of the day or ahead of a schedule — and is the natural opposite of 늦게(late). The classic confusion is 일찍 vs 빨리: 일찍 is about WHEN on the clock (일찍 일어나요 = 'wake up at an early hour'), while 빨리 is about SPEED/quickness (빨리 일어나요 = 'get up quick!'). So '일찍 오세요' invites someone to arrive at an early time, whereas '빨리 오세요' urges them to hurry. It pairs habitually with 자다, 일어나다, 출근하다, 도착하다, 출발하다. Register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 일찍/빨리 mix-up, since English 'early' and 'fast/quick' feel adjacent but map to two different Korean adverbs; also remember 일찍 is an adverb already, so you never conjugate it like the adjective 이르다.
일찍.explanation: "early" is 일찍 (iljjik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일찍 자요 ("I sleep early"). Watch the particle attached to 일찍 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
일찍.shortExplanation: 일찍 means "early" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 빨리 when you mean 'at an early hour'. 빨리 자요 means 'sleep quickly'; to say 'sleep early (in the evening)' use 일찍 자요.
Trying to conjugate it as if it were an adjective. 일찍 is the fixed adverb; you don't say 일찍어요. The related adjective is 이르다 ('to be early').
Word order: 와요 일찍 mirrors English; Korean puts the adverb first — 일찍 와요.

examples.en: I usually sleep early.
examples.note: Simple: 일찍 = at an early hour, before 자요.

examples.en: Tomorrow I want to get up early.
examples.note: Everyday: 일찍 + 일어나다 is the standard 'wake up early' collocation.

examples.en: Worried about traffic, I left thirty minutes early.
examples.note: Real situation: 일찍 here means 'ahead of schedule', and 30분 일찍 = 'earlier by 30 min'.

cluster.title: 빨리 vs 일찍 vs 어서
cluster.rule: 빨리 is about speed and 일찍 is about the clock: 빨리 오세요 means 'get here quick', 일찍 오세요 means 'come at an early hour'. 어서 also pushes for speed but sounds warm and welcoming, so it lives in polite invitations like 어서 오세요.

members.hint: about speed, and can sound impatient
about the clock, not the speed
warm urging, mostly with polite invitations

ex.ko: 자기 전에 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이기로 했어요.
ex.en: I decided to reduce looking at my phone before sleeping.
ex.note: 자기 전에 is the fixed before-sleeping frame.

자다.nuance: 자다 becomes 잘 before some future or ability forms: 잘 거예요, 잘 수 있어요.
자다.explanation: "to sleep" in Korean is 자다 (jada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 자요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 자다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 잘 자요 ("sleep well / good night.") — then reshape the same stem into 자고 싶어요 (desire), 잘 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 자요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
자다.shortExplanation: 자다 means "to sleep" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 자다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 자요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
자 주세요 is grammatically possible, but 잘 자요 is the natural phrase for “good night.” Use request forms only with a real context.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 자다 becomes 잘 수 있어요 ("can") and 잘 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I sleep early today.
examples.note: Daily routine.

examples.en: I could not sleep well yesterday.
examples.note: Common complaint.

examples.en: Shall we sleep now?
examples.note: Suggestion.

ex.en: Looking at the data, it looks like the result will change.

자료.nuance: 자료 can mean data, but in daily work and study talk it often means the file, handout, or slide deck someone needs.
자료.explanation: 자료 (jaryo) means "materials; data; documents". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자료를 보내다 ("to send the materials"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자료 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
자료.shortExplanation: 자료 means "materials; data; documents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 정보 for every kind of material. 정보 is information; 자료 is often the actual file or reference material.
Confusing 자료 with 의견. 의견 means opinion.

usagePhrases.note: Slides or handouts for a presentation.

examples.en: I will send the materials before the meeting.
examples.note: Practical work or study-group sentence.

ex.en: It is not as hard as I thought.
ex.note: This word naturally triggers realization endings because expectation changed.

생각보다.nuance: 생각보다 naturally pairs with 더라고요 because both talk about what you found after experience.
생각보다.explanation: 생각보다 (saenggakboda) = "more/less than expected". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 생각보다 괜찮다 ("to be better than expected") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 생각보다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
생각보다.shortExplanation: 생각보다 means "more/less than expected" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 생각보다 without saying what was different from expectation.
Confusing 생각보다 with 그냥 생각. 생각보다 is a comparison phrase.

usagePhrases.note: Often used with 나오다 or 끝나다.

examples.en: The food came out faster than expected, I noticed.
examples.note: Expectation plus firsthand observation.

ex.en: The teacher had the students read the passage.

읽히다.nuance: With texts, 읽히다 often describes how easily something is read or understood.
읽히다.explanation: "to be read / to make someone read" is 읽히다 (ilkida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 문장이 잘 읽히다 ("a sentence reads clearly"). Watch the particle attached to 읽히다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
읽히다.shortExplanation: 읽히다 means "to be read / to make someone read" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

입히다.nuance: 입다 is wear; 입히다 is dress someone else.
입히다.explanation: "to dress someone / put clothing on someone" is 입히다 (ipida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아이에게 코트를 입히다 ("to put a coat on a child"). Watch the particle attached to 입히다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
입히다.shortExplanation: 입히다 means "to dress someone / put clothing on someone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 입다 when the subject is dressing another person.

examples.en: The father put a coat on the baby.

설명.nuance: 설명(說明) is Sino-Korean — 說 'to tell/speak' + 明 'clear, bright' — literally 'to make clear by telling,' i.e. an explanation of how or why something works. Distinguish it from 설득(說得) 'persuasion' (talking someone INTO agreeing, sharing the 說 root) and from 묘사(描寫) 'description' (depicting what something looks/feels like); 설명 is about clarifying and informing, not convincing or portraying. As a noun it becomes the verb with 하다: 설명하다, very often softened to 설명해 주세요/주시겠어요 'please explain for me.' Collocations: 설명을 하다/듣다, 자세한 설명, 설명이 부족하다/이해가 안 되다, 설명서 'instruction manual.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'explain to me' tempts learners to mark the listener with 를 (저를 설명하다 ✗, which would mean 'explain ME'); the listener takes 한테/에게 (저한테 설명해 주세요), and what you explain takes 을/를. Bare 설명 can't be the verb — use 설명하다. Don't confuse 설명 with the look-alike 설탕 'sugar.'
설명.explanation: "explanation" is 설명 (seolmyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 설명을 하다 ("to explain, to give an explanation"). Watch the particle attached to 설명 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
설명.shortExplanation: 설명 means "explanation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Marking the listener with 를: 'explain to me' is 저한테 설명해 주세요, not 저를 설명하다 (that means 'explain me').
Using bare 설명 for 'to explain' — say 설명하다 / 설명을 하다.
Confusing 설명 (clarifying/informing) with 설득 (persuading someone) — convincing a person is 설득하다, not 설명하다.

usagePhrases.en: to explain, to give an explanation
usagePhrases.note: 설명 is a noun; 'to explain' = 설명하다 / 설명을 하다
-아/어 주세요 frames it as a favor; the polite way to ask for an explanation
자세한 'detailed' before the noun; 설명이 자세하다 puts it after
덧붙이다 = to append/add on; common in writing or talks

examples.en: Teacher, please explain it.
examples.note: 설명하다 + 주세요 = 'please explain (for me)'; softens the request

examples.en: Could you explain it one more time?
examples.note: -아/어 주시겠어요? is extra-polite; 한 번 더 = once more

examples.en: This part is a bit short on explanation.
examples.note: 설명이 부족하다 = the explanation is lacking; here 설명 is the subject (이/가)

ex.en: As for the two people, their opinions are different.
ex.note: 두 사람은 is the frame; 의견이 is the differing subject.

다르다.nuance: 다르다 is the antonym of 같다 and conjugates as a 르-irregular: the stem 다르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ and drops 으 to give 달라요 (never 다라요); past is 달랐어요. The pre-noun form 다른 is one of the most-used words in Korean and covers both 'different' and 'another' (다른 색 = 'a different/another colour'). The dangerous trap for English speakers is 틀리다, which means 'to be wrong / incorrect' — even native speakers loosely say 틀리다 for 'different' in speech, but in correct Korean 답이 틀리다 = 'the answer is wrong' while 답이 다르다 = 'the answer is different'. Mixing them can imply someone is mistaken when you only meant they differ, which can sound rude. Pair 다르다 with 하고/와 for the thing compared: 작년하고 달라요 ('it's different from last year').
다르다.explanation: 다르다 (dareuda) means "to be different". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is N하고 다르다 ("to be different from N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다르다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
다르다.shortExplanation: 다르다 means "to be different" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 틀리다 ('to be wrong') to mean 'different' — standard Korean keeps them separate; 다르다 = different, 틀리다 = incorrect, and confusing them can sound like you're calling something a mistake.
Conjugating it as 다라요 — it's a 르-irregular, so the correct present form is 달라요 (and past 달랐어요).
Forgetting the comparison particle: say '이거하고 달라요', not '이거 달라요'.

usagePhrases.note: 하고 marks what it differs from; 와/과 in writing

usagePhrases.en: it differs from person to person

examples.en: The taste is a bit different.
examples.note: 좀 softens it; note 르-irregular 달라요, not 다라요

examples.en: I think differently.
examples.note: lit. 'my thought is different' — Korean states the trait, not the person, as subject

examples.ko: 사이즈가 사람마다 달라서 입어 보고 사세요.
examples.romanization: saijeuga sarammada dallaseo ibeo bogo saseyo.
examples.en: Sizes differ per person, so try it on before buying.
examples.note: real shopping advice; 마다 + 다르다 is idiomatic

ex.en: Before starting my studying, I clear my desk.
ex.note: 공부 is a noun; 공부를 시작하다 is different from 공부하기 시작하다 but both are useful.

공부.nuance: 공부(工夫)는 한자 그대로 '공을 들여 애씀'이라는 뜻으로, 지식이나 기술을 배우고 익히는 모든 활동을 가리키는 가장 기본적인 단어예요. 비슷한 말 '학습'은 교과서나 보고서에 어울리는 딱딱한 한자어라 일상 대화에서는 거의 안 쓰고, '연습'은 이미 배운 것을 몸에 익히려 반복하는 것이라 '머리로 새로 익히는' 공부와는 결이 달라요. 영어 study처럼 목적어를 바로 붙여 '공부 Korean'이라고 하면 안 되고, 반드시 '한국어를 공부하다'처럼 -을/를을 쓰거나 '한국어 공부를 하다'로 명사화해야 해요. 동사로 쓸 때 '공부를 하다'와 한 단어 '공부하다'가 둘 다 자연스럽고, '열심히/같이/매일'과 잘 어울려요.
공부.explanation: "study, studying" is 공부 (gongbu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공부를 하다 ("study, do studying"). Watch the particle attached to 공부 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.
공부.shortExplanation: 공부 means "study, studying" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'공부하다' 자체가 이미 동사라서 '공부를 공부해요'처럼 쓰면 같은 말을 두 번 한 셈이라 틀려요. '공부해요' 또는 '공부를 해요' 한쪽만 쓰세요.
영어 'study a book'을 직역해 '책을 공부' 또는 '공부 책'이라고 하면 안 돼요. 목적어에는 -을/를을 붙여 '책을 공부하다'라고 해야 합니다.
'나는 공부를 좋아요'는 틀려요. '좋다'는 형용사라 대상에 -이/가가 붙으니 '나는 공부가 좋아요' 또는 '공부를 좋아해요'로 써야 합니다.

usagePhrases.note: 보통 붙여서 '공부하다' 한 단어로도 자연스럽게 써요
앞에 과목·언어를 붙여 무엇을 공부하는지 밝혀요

examples.en: These days studying for the exam is so tough.

examples.en: I studied together with my seatmate at the library.

ex.ko: 메시지는 보내지만 전화는 잘 안 해요.

전화.nuance: 전화 is a noun, but 전화하다 is the verb “to call.”
전화.explanation: 전화 (jeonhwa) = "phone call". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전화해요 ("I call.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
전화.shortExplanation: 전화 means "phone call" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
전화 alone is not a full verb; use 전화해요 or 전화하다 forms.

examples.en: I will call later.
examples.note: Promise.

examples.en: Can you call now?
examples.note: Question.

examples.en: Please call me.
examples.note: Request.

ex.en: Take this medicine after meals.

식후.nuance: 식후 is concise and label-like. In casual speech you can also say 밥 먹고, but at a clinic or pharmacy 식후 is the expected word. 식후 usually pairs with 에 or a time amount: 식후에, 식후 30분.
식후.explanation: "after meals" is 식후 (siku). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식후에 드세요. ("Take it after meals."). Watch the particle attached to 식후 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
식후.shortExplanation: 식후 means "after meals" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 식후 for any after-action meaning. It specifically means after meals.
Confusing 식후 with 식전. 식후 is after meals; 식전 is before meals.
Forgetting 에 in speech: 식후에 드세요 is smoother than just 식후 드세요.

재우다.nuance: 자다 is intransitive: 아기가 자요. 재우다 adds a causer: 엄마가 아기를 재워요.
재우다.explanation: "to put someone to sleep" is 재우다 (jaeuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아기를 재우다 ("to put a baby to sleep"). Watch the particle attached to 재우다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. 재우다.shortExplanation: 재우다 means "to put someone to sleep" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Saying 엄마가 아기를 자요. Use 재우다 when the mother puts the baby to sleep.

웃기다.nuance: 웃다 is what the person does; 웃기다 is what causes the laughing. In speech, 웃기다 also works like 'to be funny.'
웃기다.explanation: 웃기다 (utgida) = "to make someone laugh; to be funny". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사람들을 웃기다 ("to make people laugh") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 웃기다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
웃기다.shortExplanation: 웃기다 means "to make someone laugh; to be funny" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 웃다 when the subject is the joke. Say 농담이 웃겼어요, not 농담이 웃었어요.
Forgetting that 웃기다 can be casual and colloquial as 'funny.'
Mixing up 웃기다 with 울리다: one causes laughter, the other tears or ringing.

울리다.nuance: 울다 is cry or ring by itself; 울리다 makes someone cry or makes a sound ring.
울리다.explanation: 울리다 (ullida) means "to make someone cry; to ring". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사람을 울리다 ("to make someone cry"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 울리다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
울리다.shortExplanation: 울리다 means "to make someone cry; to ring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Saying 영화가 울었어요 when the movie made you cry. Say 영화가 저를 울렸어요.
Forgetting the object in emotional causative: 저를/사람들을 울리다.

낮추다.nuance: 낮다 is an adjective, while 낮추다 is an action verb. Compare 소리가 낮아요 with 소리를 낮춰 주세요.
낮추다.explanation: "to lower" is 낮추다 (natchuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 소리를 낮추다 ("to lower the volume"). Watch the particle attached to 낮추다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
낮추다.shortExplanation: 낮추다 means "to lower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 낮다 as an action: 소리를 낮아요 is wrong. Say 소리를 낮춰요.
Confusing 낮추다 with 내려가다. 내려가다 means go down; 낮추다 means lower something.
Forgetting the object marker: 목소리를 낮추다.

입다.nuance: 입다 is a regular verb (입어요, 입었어요, 입습니다) meaning to put on or wear clothing on the torso and legs — shirts, coats, dresses, trousers, uniforms. The thing English speakers must internalize is that Korean has no single verb for 'wear'; it splits the action by body part: 입다 for body clothes, 신다 for footwear (shoes, socks), 쓰다 for things on the head/face (hats, glasses), 끼다 for snug items (gloves, rings), 차다 for things you strap on (watch, belt), and 매다 for ties/scarves you knot. So 'wear shoes' is never 신발을 입다 — it must be 신발을 신다. A second nuance is aspect: 입다 is the action of putting on, while the resulting state 'be wearing' is 입고 있다 (티셔츠를 입고 있어요 = is wearing a T-shirt). The opposite, for taking off any of these, is the single verb 벗다. The pitfall is simply over-extending 입다 to cover everything 'wear' covers in English.
입다.explanation: 입다 (ipda) means "to wear clothes". Start from the polite form 입어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 입다. A strong first sentence is 코트를 입어요 ("I wear a coat"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 입다 also becomes 입고 싶어요 (want), 입을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 입어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
입다.shortExplanation: 입다 means "to wear clothes" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 입다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 입어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 입다 for shoes or socks — footwear takes 신다, so it must be 신발을 신어요, never 신발을 입어요.
Using 입다 for a hat or glasses — head/face items take 쓰다, so 'wear a hat' is 모자를 써요 and 'wear glasses' is 안경을 써요, not 입다.
Saying 옷을 입고 있어요 when you mean the action of getting dressed right now — 입고 있다 is ambiguous toward the state 'am wearing'; to stress the ongoing action of dressing, context or 입는 중이에요 is clearer.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 입다 becomes 입을 수 있어요 ("can") and 입을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: garments worn on the torso/legs take 을/를 with 입다

울다.nuance: 울다 means to cry and is a ㄹ irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before endings starting with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ, so the formal present is 웁니다 (not 울습니다) and the honorific is 우세요; before a plain vowel the ㄹ stays, giving 울어요 and 울었어요, and the future keeps it too in 울 거예요. The crier is the subject and takes 이/가 (아기가 울어요), unlike English where 'cry' can feel transitive. Its natural opposite is 웃다 (laugh), and its near-synonyms split by intensity and register: 눈물을 흘리다 ('shed tears', literally, more composed/quiet) describes tears running down without sobbing, while 흐느끼다 ('to sob') is heavier and more literary; plain 울다 is the everyday all-purpose word, often boosted by mimetics like 펑펑 울다 (bawl) or 엉엉 울다. Note 울다 also describes animals making their cry/call (새가 울다 = a bird sings/cries) and even a phone or alarm 'ringing/sounding'. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — writing 울습니다 by habit when the ㄹ must drop to 웁니다 — plus confusing 울다 with 웃다, which differ by a single jamo.
울다.explanation: 울다 (ulda) = "to cry". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 울어요 plus one useful sentence like 아기가 울어요 ("the baby cries"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 울고 싶어요 for what you want, 울 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 울어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
울다.shortExplanation: 울다 means "to cry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 울다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 울어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ before ㅂ and saying 울습니다 — 울다 is ㄹ irregular, so the ㄹ drops there, giving 웁니다 (and the honorific 우세요).
Confusing 울다 (cry) with 웃다 (laugh) — they differ by one jamo, so 울었어요 means 'cried' while 웃었어요 means 'laughed'.
Marking the crier with 을/를 (아기를 울어요) — 울다 is intransitive, so the one crying is the subject: 아기가 울어요 (to MAKE someone cry, use the causative 울리다, as in 동생을 울렸어요).

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 울다 is a ㄹ-stem word. The ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings: 살다 → 삽니다 (formal), 사는 (describing a noun), 사세요 (honorific). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 울어요.

usagePhrases.note: the crier is the subject and takes 이/가

ex.en: I will handle this matter.

처리하다.nuance: 처리하다 (處理하다, 處 'manage/place' + 理 'put in order') is a workhorse meaning to process, handle, or take care of a task, request, or problem, and the passive 처리되다 ('be processed') saturates official status messages. The register is neutral-professional, ideal for office work and paperwork. Watch three near-neighbors: 해결하다 ('to solve/resolve') implies fully fixing a problem so it's gone, whereas 처리하다 can just mean 'deal with / move it along the pipeline' without a happy ending; 다루다 means 'to handle/treat' in the sense of how you manage a topic or object; and bare 하다 ('do') cannot stand in for 'take care of a matter.' The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that bare-하다 trap: 'I'll do this issue' translated literally as '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong — you must say 처리할게요. Reach for 처리하다 whenever English would say 'handle,' 'take care of,' or 'process.'
처리하다.explanation: 처리하다 (cheorihada) means "to process / to handle / to deal with". Start from the polite form 처리해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 처리하다. A strong first sentence is 업무를 처리하다 ("to handle work tasks"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 처리하다 also becomes 처리하고 싶어요 (want), 처리할 수 있어요 (can), and 처리할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
처리하다.shortExplanation: 처리하다 means "to process / to handle / to deal with" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 처리하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 처리해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Learners overuse 하다 alone; '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong. Use 처리하다 to mean 'handle/take care of' a matter.
처리하다 (deal with/move along) isn't always 해결하다 (fully solve). If the issue is actually resolved, say 해결됐어요, not just 처리됐어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 처리하다 becomes 처리할 수 있어요 ("can") and 처리할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

ex.en: I'm sorry, but it will be difficult for me to attend today.

참석하다.nuance: 참석하다 is Sino-Korean 參席 — 參 'take part' + 席 'seat' — literally 'take one's seat (and take part)', i.e. attend a formal event like a meeting, ceremony, or banquet. Its register is more formal than just 가다 'to go'; you 결혼식에 가요 casually but 결혼식에 참석합니다 in polite/written contexts. Distinguish it from its close cousin 참가하다 (參加, 'participate/enter'): 참석하다 emphasizes being PRESENT and seated at a gathering, while 참가하다 emphasizes actively TAKING PART (참가하다 fits a contest, race, or program — 대회에 참가하다). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'attend THE meeting' (object) drives learners to 회의를 참석하다, but Korean uses 에 — 회의에 참석하다 — because you 'join INTO' the event. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (참석해요, 참석했어요, formal 참석합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (참석 안 해요, 참석 못 해요).
참석하다.explanation: "to attend" in Korean is 참석하다 (chamseokada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 참석해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 참석하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 회의에 참석하다 ("to attend a meeting") — then reshape the same stem into 참석하고 싶어요 (desire), 참석할 수 있어요 (ability), and 참석 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
참석하다.shortExplanation: 참석하다 means "to attend" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참석하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참석해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 회의를 참석해요 because English makes the meeting an object — Korean marks the event with 에: 회의에 참석해요.
Using 참석하다 for a contest or competition — being present at a gathering is 참석하다, but actively competing/taking part is 참가하다: 대회에 참가하다.
Forming the negative as 안 참석해요 — split it: 참석 안 해요 (impossible = 참석 못 해요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 참석하다 becomes 참석할 수 있어요 ("can") and 참석할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the event takes 에 (NOT 를): 회의에 참석해요

거절하다.nuance: 거절하다 (Sino-Korean 拒絶, 'block-and-sever') is the standard verb for declining a request, offer, or invitation, and the thing refused — 부탁, 제안, 초대 — takes 을/를. Compare it with the harsher 거부하다 (拒否, 'block-and-deny'): 거부하다 is a flat, often institutional rejection ('출석을 거부하다', 'refuse to comply'), while 거절하다 is the ordinary interpersonal 'no thanks'. Because directly refusing can feel rude in Korean social life, 거절하다 is habitually cushioned with 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), 정중하게 ('politely'), or 어렵겠어요 ('that would be difficult'); the bare verb can sound cold. A frequent English-speaker slip is reaching for 거절하다 to mean 'reject a person' romantically — that is 차다 (dump) or 까이다 (get rejected), not 거절하다, which targets the request, not the human. Also do not confuse it with 사양하다, a humble 'I'll pass' used to politely decline an offer of food or a gift.
거절하다.explanation: "to refuse / decline" in Korean is 거절하다 (geojeolha-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 거절해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 거절하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 부탁을 거절했어요. ("I turned down the request.") — then reshape the same stem into 거절하고 싶어요 (desire), 거절할 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 거절해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
거절하다.shortExplanation: 거절하다 means "to refuse / decline" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 거절하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 거절해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Do not confuse 거절하다 (decline a request/offer) with the stronger 거부하다, which feels like a flat, often official rejection.
거절하다 takes the offer as its object (제안을 거절하다); to 'reject' a person romantically Koreans say 차다 / 까이다, not 거절하다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 거절하다 becomes 거절할 수 있어요 ("can") and 거절할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I politely declined the dinner invitation.
examples.note: Note the polite-softening adverb before the verb

정중하다.nuance: 정중하다 (鄭重하다; the 重 carries 'weighty/grave,' so the word evokes treating someone with weighty respect) means courteous and respectful in a formal, dignified way — proper manners and respectful language. The near-synonym you must separate is 친절하다 (kind/friendly), and the dividing line is warmth vs. form: 친절하다 is personal warmth and helpfulness (a 친절한 점원 smiles and helps you happily), while 정중하다 is formal respect shown through correct manners and language (a 정중한 점원 is impeccably proper, not necessarily warm). For a careful apology, a polite refusal, or staff toward an important guest, you reach for 정중하다, where 친절하다 would feel too casual-warm. Also distinguish 겸손하다 (inner humility about oneself) from 정중하다 (outward courtesy toward others) — different directions. Register: 정중하다 is itself a formal-leaning word, at home in business Korean and written apologies (정중히 사과드립니다). The English-speaker pitfall is collapsing all 'polite' into one word: friendly-polite is 친절하다, formally-courteous is 정중하다. Stem note: 정중해요, not 정중하해요.
정중하다.explanation: "courteous, polite, respectful (in manner)" is 정중하다 (jeongjunghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정중하게 부탁하다 ("ask politely/respectfully"). Watch the particle attached to 정중하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
정중하다.shortExplanation: 정중하다 means "courteous, polite, respectful (in manner)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it with 친절하다 (warm, friendly kindness): 정중하다 is formal respect/courtesy shown through manners
Saying 정중하해요: the 하다 stem gives 정중해요 / 정중한 / 정중하게
Confusing it with 겸손하다: 겸손 is humility about yourself, 정중 is courtesy directed at others

결과.nuance: 결과 (結果, literally '結 form/bear + 果 fruit', i.e. the fruit that an action bears) is the end outcome of an action or event, and it almost always pairs with 나오다 (come out) or 나타나다 (appear) rather than any verb of 'making'. Its built-in partner is 과정 (the process leading up to it) and its mirror image is 원인 (the cause behind it), so Koreans constantly say 과정도 중요하고 결과도 중요하다. Register is neutral — fine in a doctor's office (검사 결과), a classroom (시험 결과), or a news report. The big English-speaker trap is twofold: first, you do not 'get' a result with a transitive verb the way English does — the result 나오다 (comes out) on its own and takes 이/가, so 결과를 나오다 is wrong; second, do not confuse the outcome 결과 with the reason 원인/이유 — 결과 is what happened at the end, never why.
결과.explanation: "result, outcome" is 결과 (gyeolgwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시험 결과 ("exam results"). Watch the particle attached to 결과 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
결과.shortExplanation: 결과 means "result, outcome" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 결과를 나오다 — 나오다 ('come out') is intransitive, so the result takes 이/가: 결과가 나오다.
결과 is the outcome, not the cause; for 'the reason/cause' use 원인 (objective cause) or 이유 (personal reason), e.g. 사고의 원인, not 사고의 결과, when you mean what triggered it.
Don't force an English plural — there is no 결과들 in 'exam results'; 시험 결과 already covers singular and plural.

손님.nuance: 손님 is native Korean — 손 'guest' + the honorific suffix -님 — so it builds 'guest' into a respectful form, and it covers BOTH a paying customer in a shop AND a guest visiting your home. That built-in 님 is why 손님 is inherently polite and why staff address you directly as 손님 (like English 'sir/ma'am'). Contrast it with the neutral 사람 'person' (too plain and even rude to call a customer) and with 고객, the more formal/corporate term banks, telecoms, and notices use (고객님, 고객 센터 customer center) — 손님 feels face-to-face and shop-floor, 고객 feels institutional. Because 손님 deserves respect, it's counted with the honorific 분 (손님 한 분, not 한 명) and described with honorific verbs (오시다 'come', 계시다 'be present', 기다리고 계세요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 사람 ('a person came to the shop' → 사람이 왔어요 sounds cold); say 손님이 오셨어요. Collocations: 손님을 받다 (take/receive customers), 손님이 들다 (customers come in), 단골손님 (regular), 손님 접대 (hosting guests).
손님.explanation: "customer" is 손님 (sonnim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 손님이 많아요 ("there are many customers"). Watch the particle attached to 손님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
손님.shortExplanation: 손님 means "customer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사람 instead of 손님 for a customer or guest. 사람이 왔어요 ('a person came') sounds blunt; in a shop or home, say 손님이 왔어요/오셨어요 to show due respect.
Counting customers with 명 instead of the honorific 분. Say 손님 두 분, not 손님 두 명 — 분 raises the politeness that 손님 implies.
Treating 손님 and 고객 as identical in tone. Use 손님 face-to-face in shops and homes; use 고객(님) for formal/written/corporate contexts like 고객 센터 (customer service center).

usagePhrases.note: 많다 'be many'; subject 이 after a consonant
분 is the honorific counter for people, raising respect
모시다 is the humble verb for serving a respected person

주문.nuance: 주문 is the noun 'order', from 注文 (注 'pour/note down' + 文 'writing') — originally 'to write down a request', which fits ordering perfectly. The verb is 주문하다, and a key contrast is 주문하다 vs 시키다: both mean 'to order', but 시키다 is more casual and also means 'to make someone do something', so toward staff the cleaner, slightly more standard choice is 주문하다 (시키다 is fine among friends: '뭐 시킬까?'). Knowing the bare noun unlocks the phrases you hear constantly — '주문 도와드릴게요', '주문 들어갔어요', '주문 확인해 주세요' — where 주문 stands alone. Register is neutral and identical in casual and formal dining. It collocates with 하다, 들어가다 (go in), 받다 (take an order), 확인하다 (confirm), and 취소하다 (cancel).
주문.explanation: "an order (of food/drink)" is 주문 (jumun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주문하시겠어요? ("Are you ready to order?"). Watch the particle attached to 주문 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.
주문.shortExplanation: 주문 means "an order (of food/drink)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 주문 (an order) with 주말 (weekend) — they look similar to beginners but are unrelated; mis-saying one for the other changes the meaning entirely.
Defaulting to 시키다 with staff ('이거 시켜 주세요') — understandable but a touch blunt; '이거 주문할게요' or simply '이거 주세요' sounds cleaner to servers.
Treating 주문 as a verb on its own ('주문 주세요') — you need 주문하다, e.g. '주문할게요', or attach 하다.
