조금.nuance: 조금 means 'a little / a bit / a few' and is the natural counterweight to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. Its closest relative is its own contracted form 좀: 조금 is the full, slightly more careful version you can write and say, while 좀 is the quick spoken reduction (조금만요 ↔ 좀만요 are the same idea). Compared with the noun-ish 약간 ('slightly', a touch more formal/written), 조금 is the warm conversational choice. It naturally collocates with quantities and gentle states — 조금 더 ('a little more'), 조금 있다가 ('in a little while') — and its softness makes it ideal for modest answers and polite requests. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 좀 in speech and not realizing it is just 조금 reduced, and over-stacking it with big-amount words: 조금 많이 is self-contradictory because 조금 only ever points to a small degree.
조금.explanation: 조금 (jogeum) means "a little, a bit, a few". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조금 주세요 ("Please give me a little"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
조금.shortExplanation: 조금 means "a little, a bit, a few" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Not recognizing that 조금 usually contracts to 좀 in casual speech; both are correct, but learners who only study 조금 get lost when they hear 좀.
Pairing 조금 with large amounts: 조금 많이 contradicts itself; 조금 is strictly a small degree, so use 많이 or 너무 for big quantities.
Confusing 조금 with 잠깐/잠시 for time: 조금만 means a small amount, while 잠깐만 specifically means 'for a short moment' of time.

usagePhrases.note: The exact opposite of 많이; requests a small amount
Before an adjective it softens the degree to 'a bit'
조금만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just a moment; 만 ('only') caps it small
A fixed time phrase meaning 'a moment ago'

cluster.rule: For real amounts all three overlap — 좀 is simply the spoken contraction of 조금, and 약간 is the cooler, more written "slightly". The deciding fact is that only 좀 has a second life as a request softener, where it means "please / if you would" and not "a little" at all (물 좀 주세요).

미리.nuance: 미리 means doing something ahead of the relevant moment so you're ready when it arrives — its whole focus is the timing being early relative to a deadline or event. The classic English-speaker trap is confusing it with 우선 / 먼저 / 일단: 먼저 and 우선 mean 'first in a sequence or in priority' (do A before B), while 미리 means 'before the due time' (do it now so it's done early). 'I paid first' = 먼저 냈어요 (before others), but 'I paid in advance' = 미리 냈어요 (before the due date) — different ideas entirely. 미리 is native Korean, not Sino-Korean, and it glues onto preparation verbs: 미리 예약하다, 미리 준비하다, 미리 확인하다, 미리 알리다. Register is neutral and works in both polite and casual speech. Note the affectionate doubled 미리미리, which nags 'do it good and early.'
미리.explanation: 미리 (miri) means "in advance, ahead of time, beforehand". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 미리 예약하다 ("to book in advance"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 미리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
미리.shortExplanation: 미리 means "in advance, ahead of time, beforehand" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 미리 for 'firstly in a sequence': 미리 이거부터 해요 is odd; for ordering steps you want 우선/먼저 이거부터 해요. 미리 only means 'ahead of the due time.'
Dropping it where the early timing is the point: 예약했어요 alone just says 'I booked'; 미리 예약했어요 adds the crucial 'ahead of time' nuance.
Saying 미리 전에 (advance + before) as a redundant pair under the influence of English 'beforehand in advance'; 미리 already contains 'before,' so just 미리 준비했어요.

후회하다.nuance: 후회하다 is Sino-Korean — 後悔 literally stacks 後 'after' + 悔 'regret/remorse', i.e. the regret that comes AFTER the deed — and names the painful wish that you had chosen differently. It typically points backward (그 결정을 후회해요 'I regret that decision') and frequently pairs with a reason clause in -아서/어서 or with a past-action nominalizer -(으)ㄴ 걸: 그렇게 말한 걸 후회해. Distinguish it from 아쉽다, which is a milder 'it's a shame / I wish it were a bit different' about things often outside your control, whereas 후회하다 carries genuine self-reproach over your own past action. Also separate it from 미안하다 ('to be sorry' TO someone) — 후회하다 is regret felt inside, not an apology directed at another person. Pitfall: 'I regret to inform you' has no 후회하다 equivalent; that polite-letter formula becomes 안타깝게도 or 죄송하지만. Keep the object with 를, and remember the negative splits as 후회 안 해요.
후회하다.explanation: "to regret" in Korean is 후회하다 (huhoehada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 후회해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 후회하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 후회 안 해요 ("I have no regrets") — then reshape the same stem into 후회하고 싶어요 (desire), 후회할 수 있어요 (ability), and 후회할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
후회하다.shortExplanation: 후회하다 means "to regret" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 후회하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 후회해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 후회하다 as an apology to someone: 너한테 후회해. To apologize you need 미안하다/죄송하다 (미안해); 후회하다 is internal regret, not 'sorry to you'.
Confusing it with mild 아쉽다. 'It's a shame the trip ended' = 여행이 끝나서 아쉬워요; deep self-blame over your decision = 그 결정을 후회해요.
Saying 후회를 안 해요 awkwardly in speech — fine, but the more idiomatic split is 후회 안 해요, and 'I'll regret it' is 후회할 거예요, not 후회겠어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 후회하다 becomes 후회할 수 있어요 ("can") and 후회할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

후회.nuance: 후회 is regret aimed squarely *backward* at a choice you already made, with a sting of self-blame. It is Sino-Korean 後悔 (後 'after/behind' + 悔 'to repent'), literally 'after-regret', the regret that comes *after* the deed. The verb 후회하다 is everyday, but the noun surfaces in lines like 후회예요 or 후회가 남아요, and the motto 후회 없이 (without regret) is hugely popular among 20-30s. The key synonym contrast is 후회 vs 아쉬움: 후회 blames *your own* decision ('I shouldn't have done that'), while 아쉬움 is a softer, fate-tinged 'aw, what a shame it didn't work out' with little self-blame. The English-speaker trap is mapping 'I regret it' straight to 후회해요 when you actually want the noun-predicate 후회예요 ('it's a regret'), and reaching for 후회 when the gentle 아쉬움 is what the situation calls for.
후회.explanation: 후회 (huhoe) = "regret". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 후회하다 ("to regret") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 후회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
후회.shortExplanation: 후회 means "regret" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 후회 with 아쉬움. 후회 carries self-blame over a choice you made; 아쉬움 is the gentler 'too bad / what a shame' with no blame. Telling a friend 후회되겠다 can sound like you're saying it was their fault.
Saying 후회해요 when you mean 'it's a regret.' For the noun-predicate use 후회예요 (or 후회가 돼요); 후회해요 is the verb 'I (actively) regret.'
Using 후회 for forward-looking worry. Regret only looks back at the past; for 'I'm worried it might go wrong' use 걱정 instead.

usagePhrases.note: the verb; 후회 itself is the noun, so for the action use 후회하다
the feeling wells up on its own; slightly passive, less self-blaming than 후회하다
the motto phrase: 후회 없이 살자, 후회 없이 도전하다
set idiom (lit. 'beat the ground and regret') for deep, too-late regret

examples.ko: 지금 안 사면 나중에 후회할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jigeum an samyeon najunge huhoehal geot gatayo.
examples.en: If I don't buy it now, I think I'll regret it later.
examples.note: Simple future hunch: 후회하다 + -ㄹ 것 같다 = 'I think I'll regret'; points forward to a choice not yet made.

examples.ko: 그때 그 집 계약 안 한 게 두고두고 후회예요.
examples.romanization: geuttae geu jip gyeyak an han ge dugodugo huhoeyeyo.
examples.en: I keep regretting not signing the lease on that place back then.
examples.note: Noun-as-predicate 후회예요; 두고두고 = 'over and over, lingeringly,' a perfect partner for regret.

examples.en: I want to give it a real try, with no regrets.
examples.note: 후회 없이 = the regret-free mindset phrase young Koreans love as a life motto.

ex.ko: 그 기회를 잡았더라면 다른 회사에 갔을지도 몰라요.
ex.en: If I had taken that opportunity, I might have gone to a different company.
ex.note: 기회를 잡다 and 기회를 놓치다 are both useful in hindsight.

기회.nuance: 기회 (機會, 機 'opportune moment/device' + 會 'meeting') is a window of opportunity that may not come twice, so it carries a faint pressure to act. The key contrast is 기회 vs 기능: 기회 is a chance to do something, while 기능 is a 'function/feature.' Koreans treat 기회 as something you physically handle — 기회를 잡다 (seize), 기회를 놓치다 (miss), 기회를 주다/얻다 (give/get) — so the partner verb is concrete, never 기회를 하다. With existence it is 기회가 있다/없다, and 기회가 되면 is a gentle, non-committal 'if the chance comes up.' The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't say 기회를 하다 by mapping 'take a chance' word-for-word, and don't mark existence with 를 (기회를 있다 ✗ → 기회가 있다 ✓). Register is neutral, fine in both polite speech and writing.
기회.explanation: 기회 (gihoe) = "chance; opportunity". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기회가 있어요 ("there is a chance") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
기회.shortExplanation: 기회 means "chance; opportunity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기회를 하다 by translating 'take a chance' literally — the verb is 기회를 잡다 (seize) or 기회를 얻다 (get)
Marking existence with 를: 기회를 있다 ✗. Existence always takes 가: 기회가 있다 ✓
Treating 기회 like 기능 (function/feature); they share 기 but mean different things

usagePhrases.note: existence takes 가, never 를: 기회가 있다
잡다 (grab) is the default verb, not 하다
좋은 modifies the noun directly, no 의
set phrase for a soft, open-ended offer

examples.en: Is there a chance?
examples.note: simplest existence frame with 가 있다

examples.ko: 저는 외국에서 일할 기회를 잡고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun oegugeseo ilhal gihoereul japgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to seize a chance to work abroad.
examples.note: a verb + ㄹ 기회 = 'a chance to do X'

examples.ko: 좋은 기회였는데 그때 안 잡아서 지금도 아쉬워요.
examples.romanization: joeun gihoeyeonneunde geuttae an jabaseo jigeumdo aswiwoyo.
examples.en: It was a good opportunity, but I didn't take it then, so I still regret it.
examples.note: real-talk: 기회를 잡다/놓치다 in past reflection

ex.ko: 먼저 사과했더라면 아직 어색하지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had apologized first, it would not still be awkward.
ex.note: 사과했더라면 fits relationship repair after the fact.

사과하다.nuance: 사과하다 is 謝過(사과)하다, hanja 謝 'express thanks/apology' + 過 'fault/error', so it literally means to 'acknowledge one's fault' — you take responsibility for a mistake to the person you wronged, who is marked with 에게/한테 or honorific 께. The boundary against 미안하다 and 변명하다 is essential: 미안하다 is the adjective/feeling 'to be sorry' (an emotional state — 미안해요), while 사과하다 is the ACT of formally apologizing (you can 사과하다 even publicly or in writing); and 변명하다 is the opposite move, to 'make excuses.' So you might 사과하다 instead of merely feeling 미안하다. The cause of the apology attaches with -아서: 늦어서 사과했어요. A notorious trap is the homograph: 사과 also means 'apple' (native-Korean noun), so context disambiguates 사과를 했어요 'apologized' from 사과를 먹었어요 'ate an apple' — they share spelling but are unrelated words. English speakers also wrongly say '~에 대해 미안해요' as if 'sorry' were a verb taking objects; to apologize FOR something, use 사과하다 with -아서 or -에 대해. Regular 하다 verb: 사과 + 해요, negative 사과 안 해요.
사과하다.explanation: "to apologize" in Korean is 사과하다 (sagwahada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 사과해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 사과하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 친구에게 사과하다 ("apologize to a friend") — then reshape the same stem into 사과하고 싶어요 (desire), 사과할 수 있어요 (ability), and 사과 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
사과하다.shortExplanation: 사과하다 means "to apologize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사과하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사과해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating 미안하다 (to be sorry — an adjective/feeling) as if it were the action of apologizing. The performative act is 사과하다: 사과할게요.
Marking the wronged person with 을/를 (친구를 사과해요). Use 에게/한테/께: 친구에게 사과해요.
Confusing the homograph 사과 (apology) with 사과 (apple), or mixing up 사과하다 (apologize) with 변명하다 (make excuses) — opposite intentions.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 사과하다 becomes 사과할 수 있어요 ("can") and 사과할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: The person wronged takes 에게/한테/께: 친구에게 사과했어요

examples.en: I'm sorry, I sincerely apologize.
examples.note: Simple: 사과할게 backs up the casual 미안해 with a fuller apology

examples.en: It was my mistake, so I apologized first.
examples.note: Everyday: -라서 gives the reason; 먼저 = first, taking the initiative

examples.en: The company formally apologized to its customers.
examples.note: Real situation: 공식적으로 (formally) + 습니다 — the register of a public apology

ex.ko: 그때 멈췄더라면 일이 이렇게 커지지 않았을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had stopped back then, this would not have gotten this big.
ex.note: 그때 anchors the regret in a specific past moment.

그때.nuance: 그때 is the demonstrative 그 ('that', the listener-known one) fused with 때 ('time, occasion'), so it points at a specific moment both speakers can already identify — looking back ('back then') or to a plan just arranged ('see you then'). Write it solid as 그때; the spaced 그 때 is non-standard. Mind the demonstrative trio that mirrors 이/그/저: 이때 = this moment / now in the flow of events, 그때 = that known moment, and the question 언제 = 'when?'. The key English-speaker pitfall is the 'that' default: because English freely says 'that time' for brand-new information, learners reach for 그때 even when the listener has no idea which moment is meant. But 그때 presupposes shared knowledge — if the time is new to your listener you must first establish it (give the date or event), and only then can 그때 refer back to it.
그때.explanation: 그때 (geuttae) = "that time, then, back then". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그때 ("that time / then") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그때, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
그때.shortExplanation: 그때 means "that time, then, back then" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing it as two words 그 때 — the standard spelling is the single word 그때.
Using 그때 for a brand-new time the listener can't yet identify — 그때 needs a shared, already-known moment.
Confusing 그때 (that known time) with 이때 (this/now) or 언제 (when?) — the 이/그/저 logic still applies.

usagePhrases.note: a moment both speakers already know
그때 + 그 + noun, e.g. 그때 그 사람

examples.en: That's when we first met.
examples.note: 처음 = for the first time

examples.en: Back then I was a student.
examples.note: 는 frames that period as the topic/contrast

examples.en: Okay, see you then.
examples.note: 그때 reused for an agreed FUTURE time

ex.en: Before memorizing words, I listen to example sentences.
ex.note: 외우기 전에 is more natural than trying to attach 전에 to 외우는 것.

외우다.nuance: 외우다 is a NATIVE Korean verb (no hanja), meaning to commit something to memory deliberately — to get it 'by heart' through effort. Contrast it sharply with 기억하다 (記憶, 'remember/recall'): 외우다 is the act of putting info IN ('I'll memorize these words tonight'), while 기억하다 is having or pulling it back OUT ('Do you remember my number?'). Mixing them is the #1 English-speaker error, because English 'remember' blurs both. A near-synonym 암기하다 (暗記) means the same as 외우다 but sounds more bookish/formal. Crucially, because 외우다 is native (not noun+하다), its conjugation differs from every other verb on this list: the stem 외우- meets 어요 and the 우 + 어 fuse to 워 → 외워요, past 외웠어요; the negative is the simple 안 외워요 and impossible 못 외워요 — there is NO noun to split off. Common collocations: 단어를 외우다, 통째로 외우다, 줄줄 외우다.
외우다.explanation: 외우다 (oeuda) means "to memorize". Start from the polite form 외워요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 외우다. A strong first sentence is 단어를 외우다 ("to memorize vocabulary"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 외우다 also becomes 외우고 싶어요 (want), 외울 수 있어요 (can), and 못 외워요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
외우다.shortExplanation: 외우다 means "to memorize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 외우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 외워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 기억하다 where 외우다 is meant: 'I need to memorize these words' is 단어를 외워야 해요, not 기억해야 해요 (which leans toward 'recall'). 외우다 = put into memory; 기억하다 = recall from memory.
Mis-contracting the 요-form as 외우어요 or 외우요 — the 우 + 어 must fuse to 워: 외워요, past 외웠어요.
Splitting the negative like a 하다 verb (외우 안 해요) — 외우다 is one native verb, so it's simply 안 외워요 / 못 외워요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 외우다 becomes 외울 수 있어요 ("can") and 외울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: what you commit to memory is an object with 를: 단어를 외워요

examples.en: I memorize words.
examples.note: Note the stem 외우- + 어요 contracts 우+어 → 워: 외워요

examples.en: I have to memorize this whole sentence.
examples.note: 다 = all; obligation ~아야 해요 → 외워야 해요

examples.ko: 단어가 너무 많아서 다 못 외워요.
examples.romanization: daneoga neomu manaseo da mot oewoyo.
examples.en: There are too many words, so I can't memorize them all.
examples.note: Native verb: impossible form is just 못 외워요 (no splitting)

ex.ko: 매일 듣는 것이 발음에 도움이 된다고 느껴요.
ex.en: I feel that listening every day helps pronunciation.
ex.note: 느끼다 can take a proposition treated as a concrete fact.

느끼다.nuance: 느끼다 (a native verb, no 한자) means to become aware of something through the senses or the heart — an emotion (행복을 느끼다), a physical sensation (통증을 느끼다 = feel pain), or an abstract impression (차이·분위기를 느끼다). The contrast with 생각하다 is sharp: 느끼다 is what your body and heart register, 생각하다 is what your mind concludes. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-using it for states: 'I feel cold/sick/tired' in natural Korean is usually the plain adjective — 추워요, 아파요, 피곤해요 — not 추움을 느껴요. Reserve 느끼다 for when you're consciously naming the sensation as an object (감동을 느끼다, 책임감을 느끼다). Conjugation: the stem 느끼 + -어 contracts to 느껴 (느껴요, 느꼈어요), never the spelled-out 느끼어요.
느끼다.explanation: "to feel" in Korean is 느끼다 (neukkida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 느껴요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 느끼다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 행복을 느껴요. ("I feel happiness.") — then reshape the same stem into 느끼고 싶어요 (desire), 느낄 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 느껴요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
느끼다.shortExplanation: 느끼다 means "to feel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 느끼다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 느껴요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying '나는 추움을 느껴요' for 'I feel cold.' Natural Korean uses the adjective directly: 추워요. 느끼다 here sounds like a clinical translation.
Writing 느끼어요 / 느끼었어요. The vowel stem contracts: 느껴요 / 느꼈어요.
Using 느끼다 for 'I feel that we should go.' That sense of 'feel = opinion' is 생각하다 in Korean: 가야 한다고 생각해요, not 느껴요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 느끼다 becomes 느낄 수 있어요 ("can") and 느낄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Emotion-noun + 을/를 + 느끼다; the feeling is the object, not an adjective.

examples.en: Are you cold? (lit. do you feel cold?)
examples.note: For bodily cold/hot Korean uses the adjective 춥다, NOT 느끼다 — a key boundary.

examples.en: I was moved by those words (lit. felt being moved).
examples.note: Past 느꼈어요; 감동을 느끼다 is a set collocation for being touched.

examples.en: I feel a lot of warmth/connection in Korea.
examples.note: 정 is an untranslatable Korean affection; 정을 느끼다 is how you say you sense it.

ex.ko: 오늘 목표는 예문 다섯 개를 외우는 거예요.
ex.en: Today's goal is memorizing five example sentences.
ex.note: Spoken 거예요 makes the action into the goal.

목표.nuance: 목표 (目標, 目 'eye' + 標 'mark/sign' — literally the mark the eye fixes on) is a concrete, measurable goal or target you aim at, and it travels with a tight verb family: 세우다 or 정하다 to set it, 이루다 or 달성하다 to achieve it. The synonym line is 목표 vs 꿈: 목표 is specific and outcome-focused (pass TOPIK 3, save 1,000,000 won, run 5km), while 꿈 is broader, emotional, and aspirational (become a doctor, a better world), so use 목표 for things you can tick off and 꿈 for the life vision behind them. Note also 목표 vs 목적(目的): 목표 is the concrete TARGET, 목적 is the underlying PURPOSE/reason. The English-speaker pitfall is forming a verb directly: 'to goal' tempts learners into 목표하다, which is unnatural in writing — say 목표를 세우다 or 목표로 하다 instead.
목표.explanation: 목표 (mokpyo) means "goal, target". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 목표를 세우다 ("to set a goal"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목표 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
목표.shortExplanation: 목표 means "goal, target" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 목표하다 in writing; prefer 목표를 세우다 (set) or 목표로 하다 (aim for).
Do not confuse 목표 (a concrete, achievable target) with 꿈 (a larger, emotional dream/aspiration).
Do not blur 목표 (the target you hit) with 목적 (the purpose/reason behind it); 'the goal is 3급' is 목표, 'the purpose of studying' is 목적.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase with 세우다 (to set up/erect); how you establish an aim
이루다 (to accomplish); reaching what you aimed for (also 달성하다)
정하다 (to fix/settle); pinning down exactly what you'll aim for

usagePhrases.en: to aim for / set as a goal
usagePhrases.note: N을/를 목표로 하다 marks the target you work toward

examples.en: My goal is to pass.
examples.note: simplest 제 목표는 N(이)에요 frame for stating an aim

examples.ko: 작은 목표부터 하나씩 이루어 나가고 있어요.
examples.romanization: jageun mokpyobuteo hanassik irueo nagago isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm achieving them one by one, starting from small goals.
examples.note: 목표를 이루다 + -아 나가다 for steady ongoing progress

examples.en: I'm studying with the goal of passing TOPIK level 3.
examples.note: N을/를 목표로 marks the concrete target you aim for

ex.ko: 꾸준히 듣는 게 말하기에도 도움이 돼요.
ex.en: Listening consistently helps speaking too.
ex.note: 꾸준히 works well with repeated -는 것 habits.

꾸준히.nuance: 꾸준히 means doing something *steadily and consistently over time, without quitting* — it is the warm praise-word Koreans reach for to describe sustainable, unglamorous, day-after-day effort. The contrast you must internalize is 꾸준히 vs 열심히: 열심히 means 'hard, with intensity/diligence' and can describe a single burst (오늘 열심히 공부했어요 = I studied hard today), whereas 꾸준히 is inherently about *continuity* across time — you cannot be 꾸준히 for one day, because the word means you kept it up. So an all-nighter is 열심히, never 꾸준히; daily practice for a year is 꾸준히. In a self-improvement context it is the natural opposite of cramming (벼락치기) or giving up. The grammar pitfall for English speakers is part of speech: 꾸준히 is an *adverb* that modifies verbs (꾸준히 공부하다), so you cannot use it to describe a noun directly — for that you need the adjective 꾸준하다 (e.g. 꾸준한 노력 'steady effort'). Habitual partners: 꾸준히 공부하다, 꾸준히 연습하다, 꾸준히 노력하다, 꾸준히 늘다.
꾸준히.explanation: 꾸준히 (kkujunhi) = "steadily; consistently (without giving up)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 꾸준히 공부하다 ("to study consistently") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 꾸준히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
꾸준히.shortExplanation: 꾸준히 means "steadily; consistently (without giving up)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 꾸준히 (consistently, over time) with 열심히 (hard, with intensity). You can be 열심히 for one day; 꾸준히 means you kept it up continuously.
Using 꾸준히 to modify a noun. It is an adverb; for a noun use the adjective form: 꾸준한 노력 ('steady effort'), not 꾸준히 노력.
Pairing it with one-off actions. 꾸준히 implies repetition over time, so 'I studied 꾸준히 last night' is contradictory — that's 열심히.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing in a study context — keep at it day after day.
For languages, instruments, sports; emphasizes regular repetition over time.
Praises sustained persistence rather than one big push.
늘다 = to grow/improve; 꾸준히 늘다 = get better bit by bit, continuously.

examples.en: I do it steadily every day.
examples.note: 꾸준히 + 하다, the most generic form of encouragement to keep going. 매일 reinforces the regularity.

examples.en: Studying steadily beats cramming.
examples.note: Direct contrast with 벼락치기. -보다 = than; -는 게 낫다 = it's better to. The classic study moral.

examples.en: If you keep at Korean consistently, you'll improve fast.
examples.note: -면 = if/when; 금방 = quickly; 늘다 = improve. Encouragement aimed straight at the learner.

줄이다.en: to reduce, to cut down on

ex.en: I decided to cut down on looking at my phone.
ex.note: The thing reduced is a concrete habit, so 보는 것을 is natural.

줄이다.nuance: 줄이다 is transitive: you reduce something. 줄다 is intransitive: something decreases by itself.
줄이다.explanation: 줄이다 (jurida) = "to reduce; to cut down on". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이다 ("to reduce phone-watching") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 줄이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
줄이다.shortExplanation: 줄이다 means "to reduce; to cut down on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 줄다 for your own action: 지출을 줄어요 is wrong. Say 지출을 줄여요.
Forgetting the object: 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이다, not just 휴대폰 보다 줄이다.
Confusing 줄이다 with 낮추다. 낮추다 is lowering a level such as price, voice, or volume; 줄이다 is reducing amount or frequency.

usagePhrases.note: -는 것 turns the action into the object being reduced.

examples.ko: 자기 전에 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jagi jeone hyudaepon boneun geoseul jurigiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: I decided to cut down on looking at my phone before sleeping.
examples.note: -는 것 is the habit being reduced; -기로 했어요 reports the decision.

ex.en: There are more people than expected.
ex.note: A changed expectation naturally takes -네요.

예상하다.nuance: 예상하다 (Sino-Korean 豫想, 'beforehand' + 'think' — to think ahead) means to anticipate or predict an outcome from reasoning: what you calculate will happen. It is emotionally neutral, which is exactly where it splits from 기대하다 (期待, to look forward to / hope for): you can 예상하다 a bad result, but you would never 기대하다 one, because 기대 carries positive hope. It also differs from 예측하다 (豫測, to forecast), which is more technical/measured (weather, data, trends), whereas 예상하다 is the everyday 'I figured this would happen.' It collocates with -(으)ㄹ 거라고 예상하다, 예상보다, and 예상이 빗나가다. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'expect' covers both neutral prediction AND hopeful looking-forward; in Korean those split, so 'I'm expecting good news (hoping)' is 기대하고 있어요, while 'I expect it'll rain (forecast)' is 비가 올 거라고 예상해요. Picking the wrong one makes you sound oddly hopeful about bad outcomes.
예상하다.explanation: 예상하다 (yesanghada) means "to expect". Start from the polite form 예상해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 예상하다. A strong first sentence is 예상했던 대로예요 ("It's just as I expected"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 예상하다 also becomes 예상하고 싶어요 (want), 예상할 수 있어요 (can), and 예상할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
예상하다.shortExplanation: 예상하다 means "to expect" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 예상하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 예상해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 예상하다 when you mean hopeful anticipation → 기대하다
예상하다 is a neutral forecast; 기대하다 means you're hoping for / looking forward to it. 'I expect good news' = 기대하고 있어요.
예상해 instead of the natural 예상돼/예상이 가다 for 'it's expected'
When the outcome predicts itself, Korean often uses the passive 예상되다: 큰 변화가 예상돼요 (a big change is expected).
예상에 instead of 예상보다 for comparison
'Better than expected' is 예상보다 좋았어요, using 보다 (than), not 예상에.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 예상하다 becomes 예상할 수 있어요 ("can") and 예상할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 예상했던 대로 = as predicted; said when reality matches your forecast

examples.en: I expected traffic since it's the weekend.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 거라고 예상하다 = predict that something will happen; the standard 'forecast that' frame

examples.en: There were more people than I thought, so my prediction was off.
examples.note: 예상이 빗나가다 = a prediction misses; here 예상 is the subject with 이

examples.en: I'd more or less expected the result.
examples.note: 예상하고 있다 = to be anticipating (ongoing); 어느 정도 = to some degree

ex.en: If I had said it clearly, there would have been no misunderstanding.
ex.note: 분명히 sharpens the missed action in a regret sentence.

분명히.nuance: 분명히 comes from 分明 (分 'divide' + 明 'bright/clear', i.e. 'distinctly clear') and links two senses: stating something plainly ('clearly say'), and asserting strong certainty ('surely, definitely'). The second floods spoken Korean, especially the exasperated 분명히 …했는데 ('I definitely did X, but…') when reality contradicts you. The sharp contrast to learn is with 확실히 (確實): 분명히 leans on the SPEAKER'S own conviction and memory ('I'm sure I did'), while 확실히 points to OBJECTIVE, checkable fact ('it's confirmed'). So 분명히 그 사람이었어 = I'm certain it was him; 확실히 그 사람이었어 leans toward 'it's been verified'. Because 분명히 voices real confidence, it clashes with a hedge — pair guesses with 아마 (probably) instead.
분명히.explanation: "clearly, surely, definitely" is 분명히 (bunmyeonghi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 분명히 말하다 ("to say clearly / state plainly"). Watch the particle attached to 분명히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
분명히.shortExplanation: 분명히 means "clearly, surely, definitely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 분명히 and 확실히 as identical; 분명히 expresses your own subjective certainty, 확실히 reports objective, verifiable certainty.
Using 분명히 for a mere guess; it claims genuine confidence, so an unsure statement needs 아마 (아마 올 거예요 = they'll probably come).
Forgetting the plain 'clearly/distinctly' meaning — 분명히 말하다 is about clarity of statement, not just certainty.

usagePhrases.note: Making your point unmistakable, leaving no room for doubt
분명히 기억나요 = I remember it for certain
Insisting something is so, often against pushback
분명히 올 거예요 = they'll definitely come

examples.en: I definitely put it right here…
examples.note: Bare, half to yourself, when something's gone missing — the classic 분명히 moment

examples.en: Please tell me clearly from now on.
examples.note: 분명히 = unambiguously; a polite request for plain communication

examples.en: You clearly said it'd be done by yesterday.
examples.note: -잖아요 reminds the listener of a shared fact; 분명히 adds insistence

당연하다.en: to be natural, obvious, no wonder

ex.ko: 연습을 많이 했으니까 잘하는 게 당연하네요.
ex.en: Since you practiced a lot, no wonder you are good.
ex.note: -네요 makes the comment a realization, not a dismissive judgment.

당연하다.nuance: 당연하다 can sound dismissive if used carelessly. 당연하네요 is softer than 당연해요 because it frames the comment as realization.
당연하다.explanation: 당연하다 (dangyeonhada) means "to be natural; obvious; no wonder". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 당연하네요 ("No wonder; that makes sense."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 당연하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
당연하다.shortExplanation: 당연하다 means "to be natural; obvious; no wonder" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 당연하다 to praise directly. For praise, say 잘하시네요; 당연하네요 explains why the result makes sense.
Forgetting that 당연히 is the adverb, while 당연하다 is the adjective.
Overusing 당연하지요 in formal situations; 당연하군요 or 그렇군요 can sound more measured.

examples.ko: 연습을 많이 했으니까 잘하는 게 당연하네요.
examples.romanization: yeonseubeul mani haesseunikka jalhaneun ge dangyeonhaneyo.
examples.en: Since you practiced a lot, no wonder you are good.
examples.note: -네요 shows the speaker is realizing why the result makes sense.

ex.en: That must have been really hard for you.
ex.note: -군요 can acknowledge someone else's experience with empathy.

힘들다.nuance: 힘들다 literally takes 힘 (strength) + 들다 ('to take/cost'), i.e. 'it costs strength', and covers anything physically OR emotionally hard, tiring, or tough — a grueling shift, single-handed childcare, a rough stretch of life. With the -기 nominalizer it labels a hard task: 공부하기 힘들어요, 참기 힘들어요 ('studying/enduring is hard'). It is a ㄹ-stem word, so the ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ/ㅅ/ㅂ: honorific 힘드세요?, attributive 힘든 일, 힘듭니다 — not 힘들세요/힘들은. The crucial contrast is with 어렵다: 어렵다 is 'difficult to understand or solve' (a hard math problem, a tricky concept), whereas 힘들다 is 'taxing — tiring or emotionally draining'. A problem can be 어렵다 without being 힘들다, and a job can be 힘들다 (exhausting) yet not 어렵다 (intellectually hard). English-speaker pitfall: English 'hard' blurs both, so learners say 어렵다 for an exhausting day — if it drains your energy or spirit, it's 힘들어요, not 어려워요.
힘들다.explanation: "to be hard; tiring; tough" is 힘들다 (himdeulda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 힘들어요 ("It's hard / tiring"). Watch the particle attached to 힘들다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
힘들다.shortExplanation: 힘들다 means "to be hard; tiring; tough" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Keeping the ㄹ in honorific/attributive forms — it is 힘드세요? and 힘든 일, not 힘들세요/힘들은.
Using 어렵다 for a tiring day — 어렵다 is 'difficult to solve/understand'; an exhausting day is 힘들어요.
Forgetting the emotional sense — 힘들다 also means a hard TIME in life (요즘 힘들어요), not only physical tiredness.

usagePhrases.en: Are you having a hard time?
I earned it with great effort

examples.en: Work is so tiring today.
examples.note: simple: subject + 힘들어요

examples.en: Living alone in a foreign place is hard.
examples.note: everyday: -기 nominalizer + 힘들다

examples.ko: 요즘 회사 다니기 너무 힘들어서 그만둘까 생각 중이에요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hoesa danigi neomu himdeureoseo geumandulkka saenggak jungieyo.
examples.en: Lately work has been so tough I'm thinking of quitting.
examples.note: real-situation: -기 힘들어서 + 생각 중

cluster.title: 힘들다 vs 어렵다 vs 피곤하다
cluster.rule: English "hard" splits in two here: 힘들다 is tough and draining (on your body or your heart), while 어렵다 is difficult to do or understand. 피곤하다 isn't "hard" at all — it describes you being tired, not the task.

members.hint: tough and draining, not puzzling
difficult — a puzzle, not a burden
tired — the person, not the task

example.en: I'm tired because I couldn't sleep.

ex.en: 은/는 and 이/가 are representative Korean particles.
ex.note: Here 조사 means a grammatical particle, not a survey or investigation.

조사.nuance: Here 조사 means the grammatical particle 助詞 ('helping word'), not 조사 調査 ('survey/investigation'). Korean particles attach to the end of a noun or noun phrase and do more than label subject, object, or location: they also manage topic, contrast, inclusion, limitation, and the speaker's focus. That is why 은/는 and 이/가 cannot be swapped mechanically, and why 에/에서 depends on the Korean predicate rather than on one English preposition. At C1, particle choice is part of information design. 제가 맡겠습니다 selects 'me' as the person who will take the task, while 저는 맡겠습니다 sets 'me' as the topic and may contrast the speaker with others. Spoken Korean can omit predictable particles, but omission is not random: a short message may say 자료 확인했습니다, while a complex or potentially ambiguous sentence often needs 자료를 확인했습니다. Particles can also stack in a fixed order—회의에서도, 이 사안에 대해서는—so a single syllable can alter both grammar and stance without changing the vocabulary.
조사.explanation: 조사 (josa) means "grammatical particle." It follows a noun phrase and signals how that phrase connects to the predicate or to the surrounding discourse. Review particles in three passes: (1) grammatical role—이/가, 을/를, 에/에서, 에게/께; (2) focus and scope—은/는, 도, 만, 까지; and (3) omission and stacking—에는, 에서도, 까지만. Do not choose a particle from an English translation alone. First identify the Korean predicate and the relationship it requires, then ask what the listener should treat as topic, new information, contrast, or addition. In final editing, two particles may both produce grammatical sentences while creating different emphasis, so 'correct' includes meaning, focus, clarity, and register.
조사.shortExplanation: 조사 is a post-noun marker that controls grammatical role, focus, contrast, scope, and clarity in Korean.
commonMistakes: Treating 은/는 and 이/가 as interchangeable subject markers. 제가 수정하겠습니다 selects the person who will do it; 저는 수정하겠습니다 sets or contrasts the speaker as the topic.
Mapping English 'at/to/from' directly onto 에 or 에서. Static location or destination usually takes 에, while the place where an action happens takes 에서: 회의실에 있습니다 / 회의실에서 회의합니다.
Using 을/를 with a verb that requires a recipient or counterpart, such as 고객님을 연락하다. Say 고객님께 연락드리다 or 친구에게/한테 연락하다.
Deleting particles simply because conversational Korean often omits them. Omit only when the grammatical role is recoverable; restore the particle when a formal or complex sentence could be misread.
Stacking particles in the wrong order, such as 회의도에서. The base relation comes first and the focus particle follows: 회의에서도, 이 사안에 대해서는.

usagePhrases.note: A final-editing action: check both grammatical role and intended focus.
Changing one particle can change contrast, scope, or the information focus.
Natural only when the missing role is clear from context.

usagePhrases.en: the focus changes with a single particle
usagePhrases.note: A useful reminder that particles carry discourse meaning, not just grammar labels.

examples.ko: ‘제가 이 부분을 수정하겠습니다’는 담당자를 특정하고, ‘저는 이 부분을 수정하겠습니다’는 다른 사람과 대비하는 느낌을 줄 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: ‘jega i bubuneul sujeonghagetseumnida’neun damdangjareul teukjeonghago, ‘jeoneun i bubuneul sujeonghagetseumnida’neun dareun saramgwa daebihaneun neukkimeul jul su isseoyo.
examples.en: ‘제가 이 부분을 수정하겠습니다’ identifies who will handle the task, while ‘저는 이 부분을 수정하겠습니다’ can contrast the speaker with other people.
examples.note: 이/가 can focus or select the subject; 은/는 frames it as topic or contrast.

examples.en: I am in the meeting room. We hold the meeting in the meeting room.
examples.note: 에 marks static location with 있다; 에서 marks the place where the action 회의하다 happens.

examples.ko: 짧은 메시지에서는 ‘자료 확인했습니다’도 자연스럽지만, 대상이 여러 개면 ‘첨부 자료를 확인했습니다’처럼 조사를 밝혀 쓰는 편이 안전해요.
examples.romanization: jjalbeun mesijieseoneun ‘jaryo hwaginhaetseumnida’do jayeonseureopjiman, daesangi yeoreo gaemyeon ‘cheombu jaryoreul hwaginhaetseumnida’cheoreom josareul balkhyeo sseuneun pyeoni anjeonhaeyo.
examples.en: In a short message, ‘자료 확인했습니다’ can be natural, but when several possible objects exist, it is safer to state the particle explicitly, as in ‘첨부 자료를 확인했습니다.’
examples.note: Particle omission depends on recoverability, not on politeness alone.

examples.ko: 이 사안에 대해서는 다음 회의에서도 계속 논의하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: i saane daehaeseoneun daeum hoeuieseo-do gyesok nonuihagetseumnida.
examples.en: As for this issue, we will continue discussing it at the next meeting as well.
examples.note: 에 대해서는 frames the issue as the topic, and 에서도 adds ‘also’ to the action location.

ex.ko: 누가 먼저 연락했어요? 제가 먼저 연락했어요.
ex.en: Who contacted first? I contacted first.
ex.note: 제가 answers 누가 with focus.

연락.nuance: 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean — 連 'connect/link' + 絡 'tie, network' — literally 'to link up,' and it covers ANY channel of reaching a person: a call, a text, a message, an email. The near-synonym to contrast is 소식: 연락 is the ACT/CHANNEL of getting in touch ('drop me a line'), while 소식 is the CONTENT/word about how someone is. Compare 통화(通話) 'a phone call (specifically)' — narrower than 연락. The crucial grammar quirk for English speakers: 연락 flips between particles. When YOU reach out it's 연락을 하다 / 연락하다 (object 를), but when contact COMES to you it's 연락이 오다 and reachability is 연락이 되다 (subject 이/가) — saying 연락을 오다 is a classic error. Also, English 'contact someone' has a direct object, so learners drop the person-marking 한테/에게: it should be 친구한테 연락하다, and incoming contact is 친구한테서/에게서 연락이 오다. 연락처 (with 처) means your number/details, not the verb.
연락.explanation: 연락 (yeollak) means "contact, getting in touch". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 연락을 하다 ("to contact, to get in touch"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
연락.shortExplanation: 연락 means "contact, getting in touch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 연락을 오다 for incoming contact — it must be 연락이 오다 (이/가), since the contact is what 'comes.'
Dropping the person particle: 'contact me' is 저한테 연락하세요, not 저를 연락하세요.
Confusing 연락 (the act of getting in touch) with 소식 (the news/word itself) — 연락이 없다 = 'they haven't reached out'; 소식이 없다 = 'no word on how they are.'

usagePhrases.en: to contact, to get in touch
usagePhrases.note: 연락 is a noun; 'to contact' = 연락하다 / 연락을 하다

usagePhrases.en: to hear from someone (lit. contact comes)
usagePhrases.note: 오다, not 을 오다 — the contact is the subject that 'comes to' you: 연락이 오다
되다 here = 'manages to connect'; 연락이 안 돼요 = 'I can't reach them'
연락 + 처(處) 'place/point' → the point at which to reach you = phone/contact info

examples.en: I'll get in touch later.
examples.note: -ㄹ게요 = a casual promise about your own action

examples.en: I heard from my friend.
examples.note: 한테서 = 'from (a person)'; 연락이 오다 takes 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: I can't reach them by call or text.
examples.note: 연락이 되다/안 되다 = to (not) get through; note 도…도 'neither…nor'

ex.en: Does that friend call often?
ex.note: 은/는 keeps the friend as the topic while asking about habit.

자주.nuance: 자주 means 'often / frequently' and describes how many TIMES an action repeats over a period — it answers 얼마나 자주 ('how often'), never how fast or how well. The frequency scale runs 항상(always) > 자주(often) > 가끔(sometimes) > 거의 안(hardly), and 자주 sits high but short of 'always'. Its natural opposite is 가끔; learners confuse 자주 with 빨리(quickly), but 자주 is about count of occurrences while 빨리 is about speed of one action — 빨리 먹어요 means 'eats fast', 자주 먹어요 means 'eats often'. Register-neutral, fine for everyone. The big English-speaker pitfall is word order: English lets you say 'I go there often' with the adverb last, but Korean glues 자주 immediately before the verb (자주 가요), and even before 안/못 in negatives (자주 안 가요).
자주.explanation: 자주 (jaju) means "often". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자주 가요 ("I go often"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자주 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
자주.shortExplanation: 자주 means "often" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가요 자주 by copying English 'I go often'. Korean adverbs precede the verb, so it must be 자주 가요.
Using 자주 to mean 'quickly', as in trying to say 'eat quickly' with 자주 먹어요 — that actually means 'eat often'. Use 빨리 먹어요 for speed.
Placing the adverb after 안 in negatives: 안 자주 와요 is wrong. The order is 자주 안 와요 ('doesn't come often').

usagePhrases.note: goes before the 안 of negation

examples.en: I eat kimchi often.
examples.note: Simple habit: 자주 sits directly before the verb 먹어요.

examples.en: These days I can't meet my friends often.
examples.note: Everyday: with 못, 자주 still comes first — 자주 못 만나요, not 못 자주.

examples.ko: 이 동네는 버스가 자주 안 와서 불편해요.
examples.romanization: i dongneneun beoseuga jaju an waseo bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: In this neighborhood the bus doesn't come often, so it's inconvenient.
examples.note: Real situation: 자주 안 와요 = 'comes rarely'; the adverb hugs the whole negated verb.

cluster.title: 잘 vs 자주
cluster.rule: These are not two shades of one word: 잘 answers "how well?" (skill, quality) and 자주 answers "how often?" (number of times), so swapping them changes the meaning entirely, not the nuance. One overlap to know: with things that happen to you, 잘 can mean "easily, tends to" (감기에 잘 걸려요 = "I catch colds easily") — but for a plain count of times, it is always 자주.

members.hint: about how well, not how many times
about how often, never how well

ex.en: Usually they send messages, but today they called.
ex.note: 평소에는 contrasts the usual pattern with today.

평소.nuance: 평소 is a Sino-Korean noun, 平素 'level-plain / ordinary times', meaning your normal, everyday baseline — the way things usually are when nothing special is going on. Because it's fundamentally a noun, it leans on particles: in conversation it's overwhelmingly 평소에 'usually', or comparative 평소보다 'than usual', or 평소처럼 'as usual'. Its job is to set a default against which you contrast today (평소보다 많아요 'more than usual'). The near-synonym 보통 普通 also means 'usually/ordinarily' and overlaps heavily; the subtle feel is that 평소 points to 'one's ordinary times/baseline' while 보통 states 'as a general rule', so 평소에 운동해요 and 보통 운동해요 are both fine. The English-speaker trap is treating 평소 like a bare adverb such as 항상 and dropping the particle — 'I usually...' wants 평소에, not lonely 평소. It's also not a verb, so never conjugate it; pair it with 에, 보다, 처럼, and attributive nouns (실력, 생활).
평소.explanation: 평소 (pyeongso) means "usually, normally". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 평소에 ("usually, in normal times"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 평소 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
평소.shortExplanation: 평소 means "usually, normally" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the particle for 'usually', e.g. ✗ 평소 일찍 자요. The idiomatic adverbial is 평소에 일찍 자요. (Bare 평소 survives mainly before a noun, like 평소 생활.)
Treating 평소 as a verb or conjugating it (✗ 평소해요). It's a noun/time word; the action comes from a separate verb after 평소에.
Forcing a 평소보다 comparison without the thing compared, e.g. ✗ 평소보다요 alone. You need both sides: 평소보다 사람이 많아요 ('more people than usual').

usagePhrases.note: The natural adverbial form — 평소 almost always wears 에 here.
처럼 'like' + 평소 = behaving the same as on an ordinary day.
보다 'than' makes it a comparison against your normal baseline.
Used attributively before a noun: 평소 실력대로 'as per usual form'.

examples.en: I usually go to bed early.
examples.note: Plain habit; the 에 is essential here for the 'usually' sense.

examples.en: Today there are far more people than usual.
examples.note: 평소보다 comparison; 오늘 (today) is implicitly measured against the normal baseline.

examples.en: I was nervous but presented calmly, as usual.
examples.note: Real situation; 평소처럼 means 'the same way I normally do'.

ex.en: Today, I contacted first.
ex.note: 오늘은 contrasts today with other days.

오늘.nuance: 오늘 usually does not need 에. 오늘에 sounds unnatural for ordinary “today.”
오늘.explanation: 오늘 (oneul) means "today". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오늘은 공부해요 ("Today, I study."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오늘 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
오늘.shortExplanation: 오늘 means "today" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 오늘에 가요 for “I go today.” Say 오늘 가요 or 오늘은 가요.

examples.en: Today, I go to school.
examples.note: Topic.

examples.en: I cannot meet today.
examples.note: Schedule.

examples.en: I study today too.
examples.note: Also.

ex.ko: 메시지는 자주 보내지만 전화는 잘 안 해요.
ex.en: I send messages often, but I do not call much.
ex.note: The object 메시지 takes 를; the contrast uses 는.

보내다.nuance: 보내다 means to send something or someone away from you toward another place or person — a message, a parcel, even a child to school — and it also carries the everyday idiom 시간을 보내다, 'to spend/pass time'. The sharp contrast is 보내다 vs 주다: 주다 (to give) is a face-to-face hand-over where giver and receiver are together, while 보내다 implies distance — the thing travels to reach the other person. So you 줘요 a gift you hand over now, but 보내요 a gift you mail; using 주다 for a text or parcel sounds like you are physically handing it across. The recipient particle is 에게/한테 (and honorific 께): 부모님께 보내다. For the 'spend time' sense, English speakers wrongly reach for 쓰다 (to use/spend money) — but time is 보내다, not 쓰다: 좋은 시간 보내세요! is the standard 'have a good time'. It is a plain native verb, regular (stem 보내- + 어 contracts to 보내, past 보냈어요), neutral register. The means/channel takes 으로 (이메일로, 택배로). Common collocations: 문자·이메일을 보내다, 소포·택배를 보내다, 시간·세월을 보내다, 사람을 보내다.
보내다.explanation: 보내다 (bonaeda) means "to send". Start from the polite form 보내요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보내다. A strong first sentence is 문자를 보내다 ("to send a text message"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 보내다 also becomes 보내고 싶어요 (want), 보낼 수 있어요 (can), and 못 보내요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
보내다.shortExplanation: 보내다 means "to send" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 주다 for things sent over a distance — 주다 is a hand-to-hand give; for a text or parcel that travels, use 보내다 (소포를 보내다).
Saying 시간을 쓰다 for 'spend time' — 쓰다 is for spending money/using things; spending time is 시간을 보내다.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 — the person you send to takes 에게/한테/께 (친구에게 보내다), while the thing sent takes 을/를.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 보내다 becomes 보낼 수 있어요 ("can") and 보낼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 문자·메시지·이메일을 보내다; the recipient takes 에게/한테.

examples.en: I send a text to my friend.
examples.note: Simple action; 에게 marks the recipient.

examples.en: Please send me the address via KakaoTalk.
examples.note: Everyday request; 으로 marks the means/channel.

examples.en: I spent the vacation at my grandmother's in the countryside.
examples.note: Real situation; the 'spend time' sense of 보내다.

ex.en: The two expressions have a difference.
ex.note: 은/는 frames the two expressions; 차이가 states what exists.

차이.nuance: 차이 is Sino-Korean (差異, 差 'discrepancy/gap' + 異 'different'), the 'difference', 'gap', or 'disparity' between two or more things. It pairs with two key verbs: 차이가 있다 (a difference exists, more static) and 차이가 나다 (a difference shows up/emerges, more dynamic, often for a noticeable gap, e.g. 실력 차이가 나다 = a clear skill gap). The thing you compare with takes ~와/과 (A는 B와 차이가 있다), and the dimension of difference takes ~에(서) (의미에 차이가 있다 = a difference in meaning). Contrast 차이 with 다르다, the adjective 'to be different': 다르다 describes that two things are not the same (A와 B는 달라요), while 차이 is the noun naming the gap itself (A와 B는 차이가 있어요) — Koreans often use 다르다 for a qualitative 'different' and 차이 for a measurable/quantifiable gap (나이 차이 = age gap, 온도 차이 = temperature difference). Don't confuse 차이 with 차별 (差別, 'discrimination'), which is unfair treatment based on a difference. Register-neutral, very common. Collocations: 차이가 있다/없다/나다/크다, 차이를 느끼다 (feel a difference), 큰 차이, 별 차이 없다 (no real difference), 나이 차이/시차 (time difference). The English-speaker pitfall: 'A is different from B' is most naturally A는 B와 달라요 (using 다르다 + 와), not A는 B에서 차이예요; reach for the noun 차이 when you mean 'the difference between/in', and the verb 다르다 when you simply mean 'differs'.
차이.explanation: "difference" is 차이 (chai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 차이가 있다 ("there is a difference"). Watch the particle attached to 차이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
차이.shortExplanation: 차이 means "difference" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 차이 like an adjective: 'A is different from B' is A는 B와 달라요 (다르다), not A는 B와 차이예요; 차이 is a noun ('the gap'), so say 차이가 있어요.
Marking the compared item with 을/를: it's A는 B와 차이가 있어요 (differ FROM B with ~와), not B를 차이가 있어요.
Confusing 차이 (a neutral difference/gap) with 차별 (discrimination) — 남녀 차이 = differences between men and women; 남녀 차별 = gender discrimination.

usagePhrases.note: 차이 + 이 with 있다, a difference exists
차이 + 이 with 나다, a difference appears between things
차이 + 이 with 크다, a large gap
~와 marks the thing compared against; 차이가 있다

examples.en: The two photos have almost no difference.
examples.note: Simple frame: A는/두 N은 + 차이가 없다/있다 to say things are (not) different.

examples.ko: 이 두 단어는 의미에 큰 차이가 있어요.
examples.romanization: i du daneoneun uimie keun chaiga isseoyo.
examples.en: These two words have a big difference in meaning.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~에 차이가 있다 (a difference IN ~), here 의미에 (in meaning).

examples.ko: 가격은 비슷한데 품질에서 차이가 많이 나서, 결국 더 비싼 걸 샀어요.
examples.romanization: gagyeogeun biseutande pumjireseo chaiga mani naseo, gyeolguk deo bissan geol sasseoyo.
examples.en: The prices are similar, but there's a big difference in quality, so in the end I bought the more expensive one.
examples.note: Real situation: 차이가 나다 in 품질에서 (in quality) driving a purchase decision.

ex.en: The truth is, I contacted first.
ex.note: 사실은 frames the correction.

사실.nuance: 사실 (事實, 事 'matter' + 實 'real/true') literally means 'the real state of a matter', so it covers both the noun 'fact' and the adverb 'actually/in fact'. Compare it with 진실: 사실 is a neutral, verifiable fact ('it rained yesterday'), while 진실 is the deeper moral 'truth' you uncover behind lies, so a courtroom seeks 진실, but a weather report states a 사실. Also distinguish 진짜, which is the casual spoken 'really/for real' and an intensifier ('진짜 맛있어!'), whereas 사실 introduces information. The phrase 사실은 / 사실 at the head of a sentence is enormously common in conversation as a gentle 'to tell the truth' before a correction or confession. The English-speaker pitfall: do not use 사실 to mean 'really' as an intensity word — '진짜 추워요' (it's really cold) is natural, but '사실 추워요' shifts the meaning to 'actually, it's cold (contrary to what you thought)'. Keep 사실 for facts and reveals, not for emphasis.
사실.explanation: 사실 (sasil) means "fact, truth". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사실은 제가 한국 사람이 아니에요. ("Actually, I am not Korean."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
사실.shortExplanation: 사실 means "fact, truth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Using 사실 as an intensifier like English 'really' (e.g. saying 사실 맛있어요 hoping for 'it's really tasty'). That actually means 'in fact it's tasty (surprisingly)'. For pure emphasis use 진짜 or 정말: 정말 맛있어요.
Saying 사실 아니에요 to mean 'that's not true'. The natural set phrase needs the subject particle: 사실이 아니에요. Dropping 이 sounds broken.
Confusing 사실 with 진실 and using 사실 for a profound, hidden truth. A detective uncovers the 진실; a footnote states a 사실.

usagePhrases.note: 사실은 at the very front softens an honest reveal, like English 'actually'
사실 + 이에요 asserts something is objectively true
사실대로 = 'as it really is'; the suffix -대로 means 'in accordance with'

usagePhrases.en: I want to know the truth.
usagePhrases.note: 사실 as the object of a verb takes 을

examples.ko: 사실 저는 매운 음식을 못 먹어요.
examples.romanization: sasil jeoneun maeun eumsigeul mon meogeoyo.
examples.en: Actually, I cannot eat spicy food.
examples.note: Bare 사실 (no 은) at sentence start = a casual 'to be honest' before a confession

examples.en: This story is not true.
examples.note: 사실이 아니다 is the set phrase for 'is not true / is false'

examples.ko: 사실은 오늘 그 얘기를 하려고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: sasireun oneul geu yaegireul haryeogo wasseoyo.
examples.en: The truth is, I came today to talk about that.
examples.note: 사실은 + a -려고 왔어요 clause reveals a hidden real reason behind an action

ex.en: The meaning is the same, but the feeling is different.
ex.note: 은/는 contrasts meaning and feeling.

같다.nuance: 같다 says two or more things match or are identical — 'A and B are the same'. To compare, the yardstick noun takes 하고/와·과 and the matching trait takes 이/가: 저하고 키가 같아요 ('our height is the same as mine'). Watch the sharp split from 비슷하다 ('similar'): 같다 means literally no difference, while 비슷하다 allows a gap — friends who 'look alike but aren't twins' are 비슷하다, not 같다. A second trap is the homophone-feeling N 같다 ('seems like N', as in 학생 같아요 'seems to be a student'), which drops 하고 and shifts meaning entirely; 같이 (together / -like) shares the root but is an adverb. English speakers also over-apply 'the same as' with 처럼 — but 처럼 means 'like/as', not 'identical', so keep 같다 for true equality.
같다.explanation: 같다 (gatda) = "to be the same". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: N하고 같다 ("to be the same as N") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 같다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
같다.shortExplanation: 같다 means "to be the same" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 같다 for things that merely resemble each other — for 'similar but not identical' use 비슷하다; 같다 claims zero difference.
Dropping the particle: native Korean is 'A하고 B가 같아요', not 'A B 같아요'. The yardstick needs 하고/와, the trait needs 이/가.
Confusing 같아요 ('is the same') with N 같아요 ('seems like N') — 학생 같아요 means 'seems to be a student', not 'is the same as a student'.

usagePhrases.en: to be the same as N
usagePhrases.note: 하고 = casual 'with/as'; 와/과 is the written equivalent

usagePhrases.en: to seem like N / to be like N
usagePhrases.note: no 하고 here — this means 'resembles', a different sense

examples.en: Our bags are the same.
examples.note: subject takes 이/가; the two items being equated

examples.en: We're the same age.
examples.note: the compared-to person takes 하고, the matching trait takes 가

examples.en: Your thinking is exactly like mine, so I was startled.
examples.note: real reaction; 랑 = casual 하고, 똑같다 raises the emphasis

ex.en: For this issue, the reason is most important.
ex.note: 중요하다 often appears with the focused subject marked by 이/가.

중요하다.nuance: 중요하다 means 'important, significant, crucial' — carrying weight, mattering a great deal. It is Sino-Korean 重要 (중/重 'heavy' + 요/要 'essential, vital'), a vivid literal image of 'heavy and essential', i.e. weighty and indispensable. The sharp contrast is with 필요하다 ('necessary/needed'): 중요하다 ranks how much something MATTERS in significance, while 필요하다 says something is REQUIRED to get a result — an exam can be 중요한 (it matters a lot) and a pencil 필요한 (you need it to take the test); they are not interchangeable. Also distinguish 소중하다 ('precious, dear'), which is emotional preciousness rather than functional weight. The collocation 중요하게 생각하다 / 중요하게 여기다 means 'to value, to prioritize'. It conjugates regularly (중요해요). English-speaker pitfall: learners blur 'important' and 'necessary' — for 'I need it' use 필요하다, reserving 중요하다 for 'it matters'; and never say 중요하요 (contract to 중요해요).
중요하다.explanation: 중요하다 (jungyohada) = "to be important". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 중요해요 ("something is important") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 중요하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
중요하다.shortExplanation: 중요하다 means "to be important" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 중요하요 instead of 중요해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Confusing 중요하다 with 필요하다. 중요하다 = matters/significant; 필요하다 = needed/required. '연필이 중요해요' (the pencil is important) usually should be '연필이 필요해요' (I need a pencil).
Using 중요하다 for emotionally precious things. For 'my family is precious to me' Koreans say 소중하다 (가족이 소중해요); 중요하다 sounds more like ranking by significance.

examples.en: This is really important.
examples.note: 반말 중요해; 이거 = casual 'this'.

examples.ko: 내일 중요한 회의가 있어서 일찍 자야 해요.
examples.romanization: naeil jungyohan hoeuiga isseoseo iljjik jaya haeyo.
examples.en: I have an important meeting tomorrow, so I should sleep early.
examples.note: Modifier 중요한 + 회의; -아서 'so'.

examples.en: I value my family the most.
examples.note: 중요하게 생각하다 = 'to regard as important / value'.

ex.en: Please contact me from the shared building entrance.
ex.note: Common in apartment delivery instructions.

ex.en: Please leave the parcel with the security office.
ex.note: 맡기다 is used when leaving something in another person's care.

ex.en: Check the directions for taking the medicine.
ex.note: A label word seen on medicine packages.
